name: Security Architecture and Engineering
plainMeaning: This domain is about building systems and buildings that are safe from the start. It covers design rules, security models, hardware protection, cryptography and physical protection.

topics.name: Secure design principles
topics.simpleExplanation: Secure design means building safety into a system from the first day, not adding it later. Think of building a house. You plan for burglars before you pour the floor. You give each person only the keys they need. You use more than one lock. Doors start locked. If the alarm breaks, the door stays shut. No single person controls everything. You keep the plan simple, and you check everyone, every time. These habits are the secure design principles.

studyNotes.heading: Threat modeling
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at threat modeling, which is where secure design begins.

Threat modeling means thinking about what could go wrong before it goes wrong. Imagine planning a family holiday. Before you leave, you ask what could spoil it. Someone could lose the passports. The flight could be cancelled. So you keep copies, and you buy insurance. You did not wait for the problem. You looked ahead.

In systems, we do this early in design, when a fix costs very little. We repeat it whenever the system changes. The work has four basic steps.

- Decide what you are protecting, and draw how the data moves.
- List the threats.
- Rank the threats by risk.
- Choose controls, and check that they work.

A well-known method from Microsoft is called STRIDE. Each letter is a type of threat.

- Spoofing: pretending to be someone else.
- Tampering: changing data without permission.
- Repudiation: denying that you did something.
- Information disclosure: leaking data.
- Denial of service: stopping others from using the system.
- Elevation of privilege: gaining more power than you should have.

Each threat attacks one security goal. Spoofing attacks authentication, which is proving who you are. Tampering attacks integrity. Repudiation attacks our ability to prove who did what. Disclosure attacks confidentiality. Denial of service attacks availability. Elevation attacks authorization, which is what you are allowed to do.

Another method is PASTA, which stands for Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis. It has seven stages. It starts from the risk to the business, and then works toward technical detail.

Here is a workplace example. A bank plans a new mobile app. The team draws the path of a payment, from the phone, to the server, to the database. At each step they ask the STRIDE questions. Could someone pretend to be the customer? Could the amount be changed on the way? They rank what they find, and they build the controls into the design.

As a manager, you want the business owner in the room, because only the owner can say what a loss would really cost.

Here is what to take away. Threat model early, repeat it after changes, and know the six STRIDE threats.

studyNotes.heading: Least privilege and defense in depth
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at two principles that limit how much damage any one failure can do.

Least privilege means that each person and each program gets only the access needed for the job, and only for as long as it is needed. Think of a house cleaner. The cleaner gets a key to the front door. The cleaner does not get the key to the safe, because cleaning does not need it.

Least privilege also applies to time. If a contractor needs access for a two week project, the access should end when the two weeks end. And it applies to software. A web application that only reads a catalogue should not connect to its database with an administrator account. If that application is broken into, the attacker gets only what the application had.

People tend to collect access as they move between jobs. This is called privilege creep. Someone moves from sales to finance and keeps both sets of rights. Regular access reviews are how a manager finds and removes it.

Defense in depth means using several different layers of protection, so that one failure does not cause a loss. A house may have a fence, a locked door, an alarm and a safe. A burglar who climbs the fence still faces the door. Each layer buys time and gives another chance of being noticed.

The layers should be different in kind. Two identical locks that open with the same key are not two layers. A good design mixes administrative controls, such as policies and training, with technical controls, such as firewalls and encryption, and physical controls, such as locks and guards.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital protects patient records. A firewall filters network traffic. Staff must log in with a password and a phone code. Access is limited by job role. The database is encrypted. Activity is logged and reviewed. Staff are trained. If a thief steals a password, the phone code stops the login. If that also fails, the job role limits what can be seen, and the logs reveal it.

Here is your takeaway. Give the least access for the shortest time, and never let a single control stand between an attacker and your most valuable asset.

studyNotes.heading: Segregation of duties and keeping it simple
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at splitting power between people, and at why simple designs are safer.

Segregation of duties, often shortened to SoD, means splitting a sensitive task so that one person cannot finish it alone. You will also hear it called separation of duties. Think about a club treasurer. One member writes the cheque, and a second member must also sign it. The treasurer cannot quietly pay herself.

Here is a workplace example. In an accounts office, one clerk sets up a new supplier, and a different clerk approves payments to suppliers. If one person could do both, that person could invent a fake supplier and pay it. With the duties split, cheating needs collusion, which means two or more people working together dishonestly. Collusion is harder to arrange and easier to discover.

This principle is close to two others, so let us keep them apart. Segregation of duties splits one task between people, all of the time. Two person control means two people must act together at the moment of a critical action, such as opening a vault. Job rotation moves people between roles over time, so that hidden fraud comes to light when someone new takes over.

What about a very small team, where there are not enough people to split the work? Then use a compensating control, which is an alternative that reduces the same risk. For example, a manager might review every payment log each week.

Now to the second idea, keep it simple and small. Complex systems contain more mistakes, and they are harder to test. Think about a door with one good lock, compared with a door that has a complicated mechanism nobody understands. The more moving parts there are, the more can go wrong.

Simple design also shrinks the attack surface, which is every place an attacker could try to get in. Every extra feature, open port or unused account is another door to guard. So remove what you do not need.

A manager should question every added feature, and ask whether it is worth the extra risk.

Here is what to take away. Split sensitive tasks so that fraud needs collusion, and keep designs small enough that you can actually check them.

studyNotes.heading: Secure defaults and failing securely
studyNotes.body:
Next, we are going to look at how a system should behave when it is first switched on, and how it should behave when it breaks.

Secure defaults means a product is safe straight out of the box. Extra services are turned off. Guest access is turned off. Default passwords must be changed at first use. People have to make a choice to open things up. Think of a new bank account where online transfers are switched off until you ask for them. If you do nothing, you are still safe.

This matters because most people never change the settings they were given. Whatever the default is, that is what most systems will run with.

Fail securely means that when something breaks, it ends up in a safe state. If a login server crashes, nobody gets in. If a firewall, the gatekeeper of a network, fails, it blocks traffic. You will also hear this called failing closed. The same applies to software. If a program hits an error while checking permissions, the answer must be no. It must also avoid showing a detailed error message that helps an attacker.

Now here is a detail that the exam tests. In physical security, two terms have exact meanings.

- Fail-safe: when power is lost, the door unlocks, so that people can get out.
- Fail-secure: when power is lost, the door stays locked, so that assets stay protected.

So the words sound similar but protect different things. Fail-safe protects people. Fail-secure protects property. Whenever people may be inside, life safety wins. A fire exit must let people out during a power failure, even though that weakens security.

Here is a workplace example. A company has a records room with a magnetic door lock. The fire code requires that anyone inside can always leave. So the door releases from the inside, while an alarm sounds and a camera records who went through it. The company has kept people safe and has still detected the event.

A good manager does not choose between safety and security. A good manager puts safety first, and then adds other controls to manage the risk that remains.

Here is your takeaway. Start safe, fail safe, and when a door has to choose between a person and a server, the person wins.

studyNotes.heading: Zero trust and trust but verify
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will compare two ways of thinking about trust. The older way is called trust but verify. The newer way is called zero trust.

Trust but verify works like an office with a guard at the front door. Once you are past the guard, you can walk around freely. Your actions may be checked later, through logs and audits. In a network, this meant that anyone inside the company network was trusted. The danger is obvious. One stolen laptop or one tricked employee puts an attacker on the inside, where nobody is checking.

Zero trust means never trust, always verify. Being inside the building or the network earns you nothing. Every request is checked, every time. Who is asking? From which device? Is that device healthy and up to date? What are they asking for, and do they need it?

Think about an airport. You show your passport at check-in, and again at security, and your boarding pass again at the gate. Getting through one checkpoint does not excuse you from the next.

Zero trust is a way of designing, and it is not a product you can buy. Be careful if a vendor tells you otherwise. NIST, the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology, describes it in Special Publication 800-207. That publication separates two jobs. A policy decision point decides whether a request is allowed. A policy enforcement point carries out that decision, by opening or closing the path.

A zero trust design relies on three habits. Use strong identity checks, including multi-factor authentication, which means proving who you are in more than one way. Grant least privilege for each request. And use microsegmentation, which splits the network into very small zones, so that an intruder cannot move around freely.

Here is a workplace example. A company has staff working from home and from the office. In the old design, the office network was trusted. In the new design, a laptop in the office goes through the same checks as a laptop at home. If the laptop has missing updates, access to the finance system is refused.

Here is what to take away. Trust but verify checks later and trusts by location, while zero trust checks every request and never trusts by location.

studyNotes.heading: Privacy by design, shared responsibility and SASE
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at three more ideas from the outline: privacy by design, shared responsibility, and something called SASE.

Privacy by design means planning for privacy from the very start, and not bolting it on later. Collect only the data you need. Make the private choice the default. Protect the data for its whole life, and be open with people about what you do with it. Here is an everyday example. A school app that only sends homework has no reason to ask for a parent's income, so it should not ask.

In the workplace, imagine a retailer designing a loyalty scheme. The team decides to store a member number and a postcode area, and not a full address or a date of birth. They also set a date for deleting old records. Data that was never collected can never be leaked.

Shared responsibility means that security duties are split between parties, such as a company and its cloud provider. It is like renting a flat. The landlord keeps the building sound. You lock your own door. Write the split down in the contract, so that nobody assumes the other side is doing it. Gaps usually appear where each side thought the other was responsible. Even when a task is handed over, the company stays accountable for its own data.

Now to SASE, which is usually said as sassy. It stands for Secure Access Service Edge. It joins networking and security into one service delivered from the cloud, close to the user. It combines these parts.

- Software-defined wide area networking, which makes smart links between sites.
- A secure web gateway, which filters web traffic.
- A cloud access security broker, which controls the use of cloud applications.
- A firewall delivered as a service.
- Zero trust network access, which checks each connection.

Imagine a company with forty small branches and many people working from home. In the past, all traffic had to travel back to head office to be inspected. With SASE, each user connects to a nearby cloud point, and the security is applied there.

As a manager, ask for these principles at the start of a project, and get leadership support for them in policy.

Here is your takeaway. Design privacy in, write responsibilities down, and think of SASE as networking and security delivered together from the cloud.

topics.memoryHook: A safe house: plan for burglars (threat model), few keys (least privilege), many locks (depth), two signatures (SoD), door stays shut if the alarm dies (fail secure).

question.prompt: A school is designing a new grades system. In a design review, a developer asks what the grade-change page should do if the permission-checking service stops responding. What is the BEST design choice?
options: Allow the change and write a note in the log for later review
Let teachers continue, because they are trusted members of staff
Refuse the change until the permission check is working again
Show an error and let the user retry with a shared admin password
question.explanation: Failing securely means that when a safety check breaks, access is refused. Allowing the change and logging it is tempting because work continues, but it lets unchecked changes through. Grades are not a life-safety issue, so there is no reason to open the door.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A project manager plans to carry out threat modeling on a new payroll application six months after it goes live, so that real attacks can guide the work. What should the security manager advise?
options: Keep the plan, because live attack data is the most accurate source
Skip the exercise, because a penetration test will cover the same ground
Begin during design, and repeat it whenever the system changes
Hand the exercise to the vendor and ask for a signed statement
practiceQuestions.explanation: Threat modeling belongs early in design, when fixes are cheap, and it is repeated after changes. Waiting for live attack data is tempting, but by then the design flaws are already built in and costly to fix.

practiceQuestions.prompt: While buying goods from an online shop, a customer intercepts the web request on its way to the server and lowers the price field. Which STRIDE threat BEST describes this?
options: Tampering
Spoofing
Repudiation
Elevation of privilege
practiceQuestions.explanation: Changing data without permission is tampering. Elevation of privilege is tempting because the customer got something they should not have, but no extra rights were gained. The data itself was altered.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A help desk analyst must cover a colleague's password reset duties for two weeks. Which approach BEST applies least privilege?
options: Add the analyst to the administrators group until the colleague returns
Let the analyst use the colleague's account for the two weeks
Copy every permission the colleague holds to the analyst permanently
Grant only the password reset right, with a fixed end date
practiceQuestions.explanation: Least privilege means only the access needed, for only as long as needed. Adding the analyst to the administrators group is tempting because it is quick, but it grants far more power than the task requires.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An audit finds that one clerk in a purchasing team can both create new suppliers and approve payments to them. What is the BEST corrective action?
options: Assign supplier creation and payment approval to different people
Require the clerk to change their password every thirty days
Send the clerk on an ethics course and record that they attended
Encrypt the supplier table inside the purchasing database
practiceQuestions.explanation: Splitting the two duties means fraud would need collusion. Ethics training is tempting because it addresses behaviour, but it leaves one person able to create and pay a fake supplier.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A vendor ships a network device with remote administration switched on, a guest account enabled and a published default password. Which design principle does this MOST clearly break?
options: Defense in depth
Secure defaults
Segregation of duties
Shared responsibility
practiceQuestions.explanation: A product should be safe when first switched on, with extras turned off. Defense in depth is tempting because more layers would help, but the direct fault is the unsafe starting state.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A door on a building's emergency escape route is designed to unlock automatically whenever electrical power is lost. Which term describes this behaviour?
options: Fail-secure
Secure by default
Fail-safe
Least privilege
practiceQuestions.explanation: Fail-safe means the door unlocks on power loss, so that people can escape. Fail-secure is tempting because the word secure sounds right, but that term means the door stays locked to protect assets.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An attacker tricks one employee and gets past the company's single strong firewall. Nothing else stands in the way, and the attacker reads every file server. Which principle was MOST lacking?
options: Privacy by design
Secure defaults
Trust but verify
Defense in depth
practiceQuestions.explanation: One control failed and nothing stood behind it, which is what layered defense prevents. Trust but verify is tempting, but it is the older model that trusts people inside the network, which is part of this problem.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A hospital wants to adopt a zero trust approach for its patient records application. Which design BEST reflects that approach?
options: Staff on the hospital network connect without a further login
Each request is checked for user, device health and need
All remote staff connect through one large virtual private network
Logs are reviewed every month to look for unusual access
practiceQuestions.explanation: Zero trust verifies every request and gives location no credit. The monthly log review is tempting because checking is good, but checking later is the trust but verify model.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A fitness app needs only step counts to work, but the marketing team also wants each user's home address and employer collected in case they are useful later. What should the security manager recommend?
options: Collect only the data the service actually needs
Collect all of it, but encrypt it while it is stored
Collect all of it, and explain this in the privacy notice
Collect it for one year, and review its usefulness after that
practiceQuestions.explanation: Privacy by design means collecting only what is needed. Encrypting everything is tempting because it sounds protective, but the safest data is data that was never gathered.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has many small branches and a large number of home workers. It wants network links, web filtering, a firewall and zero trust access delivered together from the cloud, close to each user. Which approach BEST fits?
options: A second data centre with extra firewalls
A virtual private network back to head office
A public key infrastructure for every branch
Secure Access Service Edge
practiceQuestions.explanation: SASE combines networking and security in one cloud-delivered service near the user. A virtual private network is tempting because it serves remote staff, but it sends traffic back to one place and does not provide the combined service.

topics.name: Security models
topics.simpleExplanation: A security model is a strict set of rules for who may do what to which information. Some models protect secrets. Some protect correctness. Bell-LaPadula is about keeping secrets. Biba is about keeping data correct. Clark-Wilson makes people use approved programs instead of touching data directly. Brewer-Nash stops conflicts of interest. Others describe safe states and how information may flow. For the exam, know each model's goal and its rules, especially which direction of reading and writing is banned.

studyNotes.heading: What a model is, and the two ideas underneath
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at what a security model actually is, and at two ideas that sit beneath many of the models.

A policy says what we want. A security model turns that goal into exact rules. A system is then built to follow those rules. Think of a family rule that says the children must be safe online. That is the policy. The model is the precise set of rules: this child may visit these sites, at these times, and no others.

Two words appear everywhere in this topic. A subject is an active thing, such as a person or a program. An object is a passive thing, such as a file. Subjects act on objects.

Now, a model is not software you can install. It is a design idea. A security architect uses it to decide how a system should behave.

The first underlying idea is the state machine model. A state is a snapshot of a system at one moment. The model says this. If a system starts in a secure state, and every change keeps it in a secure state, then the system is always secure. Think of a bank vault with a rule that the door can only move from locked to open when two managers are present. If it starts locked, and every change obeys the rule, it can never reach an unsafe condition. Bell-LaPadula, which we will meet next, is built on this idea.

The second idea is the lattice model. A lattice is a grid of levels. Every subject and every object has a place on it. For each pair, there is a highest level that the subject can reach, called the upper bound, and a lowest level, called the lower bound.

In the workplace, imagine a government office with levels called Confidential, Secret and Top Secret. An officer cleared for Secret has Secret as the upper bound for reading. The grid gives an exact answer to the question: may this subject touch this object?

A simpler tool that you will also see is the access control matrix. It is a grid with subjects down the side and objects across the top. Each cell lists the allowed actions.

Here is what to take away. A model turns a goal into exact rules, a subject acts on an object, and a state machine starts secure and stays secure.

studyNotes.heading: Bell-LaPadula: keeping secrets
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the first model you must know exactly, which is Bell-LaPadula.

Bell-LaPadula protects confidentiality, which means keeping secrets. It came from military needs in the 1970s. It is a state machine model that uses levels, and it is mainly about how information can move between those levels. It has these rules.

- Simple security property: no read up. You may not read above your level.
- Star property: no write down. You may not write to a lower level.
- Strong star property: you may read and write only at your own level.
- Discretionary security property: an access table also controls who may do what.

Let us take the first two slowly, because they are the most tested.

No read up is the obvious one. A person cleared for Secret must not read Top Secret. Think of a junior employee who must not open the directors' salary file.

No write down is less obvious. Why stop someone writing to a lower level? Because a person at a high level could copy a secret into a low level document, where lower-cleared people could read it. It also stops a malicious program, running with a high level user's rights, from quietly leaking secrets downward.

So you may be surprised to learn that writing up is allowed. A junior officer may write a report for a senior officer. Information moves upward, which is safe for secrecy. The junior officer may not then read it back.

A word about exceptions. A trusted subject is a carefully controlled process that is allowed to break the star property, for example to declassify a document that is no longer secret.

Here is a workplace example. An analyst at the Secret level opens a Secret report and tries to paste a paragraph into a Confidential memo. The system refuses, because that would be writing down.

Now the limits. Bell-LaPadula handles confidentiality only. It says nothing about integrity, so someone at a low level could write nonsense into a high level file. It also says nothing about availability.

Here is your takeaway. Bell-LaPadula keeps secrets. Simple means no read up, and star means no write down. Remember too that simple is always about reading, and star is always about writing.

studyNotes.heading: Biba, the star rules and a worked comparison
studyNotes.body:
Next we will look at Biba, and then we will put it side by side with Bell-LaPadula, so that you never mix them up.

Biba protects integrity, which means keeping data correct. Its rules are the opposite of the rules we have just learned. It has these rules.

- Simple integrity property: no read down. Do not rely on less trusted data.
- Star integrity property: no write up. Do not spoil more trusted data.
- Invocation property: a subject may not call on a subject at a higher integrity level.

Here is an everyday way of thinking about it. You are a doctor. You should not base your treatment on a rumour from a social media post. That is no read down. And a patient's neighbour must not be allowed to write in the patient's medical chart. That is no write up.

In the workplace, picture a company's finance system. The official ledger has high integrity. A spreadsheet emailed around by staff has low integrity. Under Biba, the ledger process must not read figures from that spreadsheet, and a staff member at a low integrity level must not write directly into the ledger.

The outline also mentions the Star Model. Study it as these star rules, which are the rules that control writing in both models.

Now the worked comparison. Sam works at the Medium level. There are also Low and High levels.

Under Bell-LaPadula, Sam may read Low and Medium. Sam may not read High. Sam may write Medium and High. Sam may not write Low.

Under Biba, Sam may read Medium and High. Sam may not read Low. Sam may write Medium and Low. Sam may not write High.

This is a useful way to hold it in mind. Secrets must not travel down. So in Bell-LaPadula, you can look down and you can write up. Dirt must not travel up. So in Biba, you can look up and you can write down.

Both models leave things out. Neither handles availability. Bell-LaPadula ignores integrity, and Biba ignores confidentiality. Biba also deals only with stopping unauthorized people from changing data. It does not stop authorized people from making improper changes.

Here is what to take away. Bell keeps secrets, with no read up and no write down. Biba keeps data correct, with no read down and no write up.

studyNotes.heading: Clark-Wilson: integrity through approved programs
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at Clark-Wilson, the integrity model most suited to business systems.

Clark-Wilson says that users must never touch important data directly. They must go through an approved program. Think of a bank. You cannot walk into the vault and change your balance. A teller uses the banking system, and that system follows rules. You are the subject, the banking software is the program, and your balance is the object.

That link of three is called the access triple: subject, program, object. It is the phrase to remember.

Clark-Wilson has its own vocabulary, and the exam may use it.

- CDI, or Constrained Data Item: protected data, such as an account balance.
- UDI, or Unconstrained Data Item: unchecked data, such as text typed by a user.
- TP, or Transformation Procedure: the approved program that changes data.
- IVP, or Integrity Verification Procedure: a check that the data is still correct.

It also enforces two practices. The first is well-formed transactions. A well-formed transaction takes data from one correct state to another correct state. Moving money means taking it from one account and adding it to another, and both halves must happen. The second is separation of duties, so that the person who enters a change is not the person who approves it.

Clark-Wilson goes further than Biba. It works toward three integrity goals.

- Prevent unauthorized users from making changes.
- Prevent authorized users from making improper changes.
- Keep the data consistent, inside the system and with the real world.

Biba deals only with the first goal. This is a frequent exam distinction.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital's laboratory system stores blood results. A technician enters a result through the approved laboratory application. The application checks that the number is sensible. A senior scientist must approve it before it reaches the patient's record. Nobody edits the database directly. Every night, a separate job checks that the stored results still match the instrument readings. That job is the Integrity Verification Procedure.

So if an exam scenario describes people changing data only through a controlled application, along with split duties, think of Clark-Wilson.

Here is your takeaway. Clark-Wilson protects integrity through the access triple of subject, program and object, along with well-formed transactions and separation of duties.

studyNotes.heading: Brewer-Nash, Take-Grant and Graham-Denning
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to look at three models that handle very different problems: conflicts of interest, and how rights are passed around.

Brewer-Nash is also called the Chinese Wall model. It prevents conflicts of interest. What makes it special is that access changes based on what you have already seen. It is dynamic, which means it changes over time.

Think of a lawyer in a town with two rival shops. Before taking either case, the lawyer could work for either. Once she has read the private papers of the first shop, she must not read the papers of the second.

In the workplace, a consultant who opens Bank A's files is then blocked from rival Bank B's files. The consultant can still open files for an airline, because an airline is not a competitor of Bank A. Companies that compete are grouped into what is called a conflict of interest class. Within a class, you may see only one company's data.

So do not confuse this with Bell-LaPadula. Levels do not change in Bell-LaPadula. In Brewer-Nash, your own history decides what you can do next.

Take-Grant uses a drawing of arrows, called a directed graph, to show how rights move between subjects and objects. It has four rules.

- Take: a subject takes rights from another.
- Grant: a subject gives rights to another.
- Create: a subject makes a new object.
- Remove: a subject removes rights it holds.

Its practical use is to answer one question. Could this user ever end up with this right, by following a chain of takes and grants?

Graham-Denning sets out how subjects and objects should be securely created and deleted, and how rights are assigned. It defines eight basic protection rights. They include creating and deleting objects and subjects, and reading, granting, deleting and transferring an access right. A related model, Harrison-Ruzzo-Ullman, looks at whether rights can be changed safely, and it asks whether a subject could ever obtain a particular right.

Here is a workplace example of why this matters. An employee who may hand their own rights to a colleague can spread access far beyond what anyone intended.

Here is what to take away. Brewer-Nash reacts to what you have seen, and Take-Grant and Graham-Denning describe how rights are created and passed on.

studyNotes.heading: Information flow, noninterference and choosing a model
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at models concerned with how information flows, and then at how to choose the right model in an exam question.

The information flow model tracks how information moves from one security level to another. Only authorized flows are allowed. Bell-LaPadula and Biba can both be seen as information flow models, because they control which direction data may travel.

The noninterference model is stricter. It says that actions at a high level must not affect what a lower level can see. If a low level user can notice high level activity, information has leaked.

Think about two flats that share a wall. You must not be able to tell what your neighbour is doing, not from noise and not from anything else. If you can tell they are at home because your lights dim whenever they use the oven, then something has leaked.

This model helps to defend against covert channels, which are hidden ways of passing information. Imagine a program at a high level that makes the processor busy for one second to signal a one, and idle for one second to signal a zero. A program at a low level, timing its own speed, could read that message. Nothing was written down, but a secret travelled anyway.

Three other names may appear. Goguen-Meseguer is an integrity model built on noninterference. Sutherland is an integrity model that uses states and information flow to prevent interference. You need only recognise these.

Now, how do you choose in a scenario? Ask what the question is really protecting. If the concern is secrets at fixed levels, think of Bell-LaPadula. If the concern is keeping data correct at fixed levels, think of Biba. If the concern is that changes go through approved programs, with duties split, think of Clark-Wilson. If the concern is competing clients, think of Brewer-Nash. If the concern is how rights spread, think of Take-Grant.

Here is a workplace example. An accountancy firm has several banks as clients. Partners ask for a control that stops an auditor who has worked on one bank from seeing another bank's working papers. That is a conflict of interest problem, so the model is Brewer-Nash.

Here is your takeaway. Noninterference means high level actions leave no trace at low levels, and the right model is the one that matches what the scenario is protecting.

keyTerms.meaning: A subject acts, such as a user. An object is acted on, such as a file.
Confidentiality model: no read up, no write down.
Integrity model: no read down, no write up.
The rule in these models that controls writing.
Integrity model where users change data only through approved programs.
Clark-Wilson link of subject, program and object.
Chinese Wall model: blocks access that would create a conflict of interest.
Model that shows how rights are passed, using a directed graph.
Starts secure and stays secure through every change.
High-level actions must not change what low levels can see.

keyPoints: Bell-LaPadula protects secrets: no read up, no write down.
Biba protects correctness: no read down, no write up.
Clark-Wilson forces all changes through approved programs.
Brewer-Nash changes access to prevent conflicts of interest.
topics.memoryHook: Bell keeps secrets, Biba keeps it correct. Simple is always about reading, star is always about writing.

question.prompt: A consulting firm advises two competing airlines. After an analyst opens confidential files for the first airline, the system automatically blocks that analyst from the second airline's files. Which model does this BEST describe?
options: Brewer-Nash
Bell-LaPadula
Biba
Take-Grant
question.explanation: Brewer-Nash changes access based on what a person has already seen, to stop a conflict of interest. Bell-LaPadula is tempting because the files are confidential, but it uses fixed levels and does not react to earlier access.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An analyst cleared to Secret tries to copy a paragraph from a Secret report into a Confidential memo. The system blocks it. Which rule has been enforced?
options: The Biba simple integrity property
The Bell-LaPadula simple security property
The Biba invocation property
The Bell-LaPadula star property
practiceQuestions.explanation: Writing Secret content to a lower level breaks the star property, which is no write down. The simple security property is tempting, but simple is about reading, and this action is a write.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Under Bell-LaPadula, a user cleared at the Confidential level wants to perform an action on a Secret document. Which action does the model allow?
options: Add a section to the document
Read the document in full
Read the summary page only
Copy the document to Confidential
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bell-LaPadula forbids reading up and writing down, so writing up is allowed. Reading the summary is tempting because it seems a small request, but any reading above your level is forbidden.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A pharmaceutical firm wants to make sure that a highly trusted dosage process never draws on figures from an unverified staff spreadsheet. Which rule MOST directly addresses this?
options: Bell-LaPadula no read up
Bell-LaPadula no write down
Biba no read down
Biba no write up
practiceQuestions.explanation: A trusted process must not rely on less trusted data, which is Biba's no read down. Biba's no write up is tempting because it also protects integrity, but it stops low level subjects from writing to high level data, and here the trusted process is the reader.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Maria works at the Medium integrity level in a system that enforces Biba. Which action is permitted?
options: Reading a Low integrity file
Writing to a High integrity file
Reading a High integrity file
Calling a High integrity process
practiceQuestions.explanation: Biba forbids reading down and writing up, so reading upward is allowed. Calling a High integrity process is tempting because it feels like asking for help, but the invocation property forbids it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A retailer requires that stock figures be changed only through a tested stock application, never by editing the database, with a second person approving large changes. Which model BEST fits?
options: Clark-Wilson
Biba
Take-Grant
Noninterference
practiceQuestions.explanation: Forcing every change through an approved program, with separated duties, is Clark-Wilson. Biba is tempting because it also protects integrity, but it uses integrity levels and does not require approved programs or separated duties.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In Clark-Wilson terms, which item is the check that runs each night to confirm that protected account data is still correct?
options: Constrained Data Item
Integrity Verification Procedure
Transformation Procedure
Unconstrained Data Item
practiceQuestions.explanation: An Integrity Verification Procedure checks that protected data remains correct. A Transformation Procedure is tempting because it is also a process, but it is the approved program that changes the data.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security architect must show whether a junior user could ever end up with a sensitive right by following a chain of permissions passed between accounts. Which model is MOST useful?
options: Bell-LaPadula
Take-Grant
Brewer-Nash
Biba
practiceQuestions.explanation: Take-Grant uses a directed graph to show how rights can move between subjects and objects. Brewer-Nash is tempting because access changes in it too, but it is about conflicts of interest and not about chains of rights.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A system at a high level changes how busy the processor is, and a program at a lower level can detect the change. Which model does this behaviour MOST directly break?
options: Take-Grant
Clark-Wilson
Graham-Denning
Noninterference
practiceQuestions.explanation: Noninterference says high level actions must not affect what lower levels can see. Graham-Denning is tempting because it is a formal model, but it deals with creating subjects and objects and assigning rights.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A law firm's system lets a new associate open either of two competing clients' files, but blocks the second client as soon as the first has been opened. Which feature of the model makes this possible?
options: Access depends on the fixed clearance of the associate
Access depends on what the associate has already seen
Access depends on a formal chain of granted rights
Access depends on the approved program being used
practiceQuestions.explanation: Brewer-Nash is dynamic, so access reacts to earlier access. Fixed clearance is tempting because it is how most classified systems work, but a fixed clearance would not change after the first file was opened.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security manager is told that a system fully enforces Bell-LaPadula. Which additional concern should the manager still raise?
options: Junior staff may read documents above their clearance
Staff at high levels may copy secrets to lower levels
Data could be wrongly changed by those at lower levels
Files could be labelled with more than one clearance
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bell-LaPadula covers confidentiality only, so integrity is not addressed and writing up is allowed. The first two options are tempting, but those are precisely the actions the model already prevents.

topics.name: Choosing controls and evaluating systems
topics.simpleExplanation: Before you buy a lock, you decide what it must protect. Security works the same way. First write down the system's security requirements, based on risk, laws and business needs. Then choose controls that meet them at a sensible cost. To trust a product, you can look for independent testing. Common Criteria is an international testing scheme. It gives products an Evaluation Assurance Level, from 1 to 7. A higher level means deeper testing, not more features.

studyNotes.heading: Controls come from requirements
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at where security controls should come from. The answer is requirements, and not from a favourite product.

A control is anything that reduces risk, such as a password rule, a guard or a backup. Imagine buying a lock for a shed. Before you go to the shop, you ask what is in the shed, who might want it, and what the insurance company requires. A garden fork needs one kind of lock. An expensive motorcycle needs another. If you buy the most impressive lock first and think later, you may have wasted your money.

System security requirements come from several places.

- Risk assessments, which tell us what could go wrong and how badly.
- Laws and regulations.
- Contracts with customers and suppliers.
- Company policy.
- Business goals.

There are two kinds of requirement, and the exam expects you to tell them apart.

A functional requirement says what the control must do. For example, lock an account after five bad passwords.

An assurance requirement says how sure we are that it works. For example, an independent laboratory has tested the product.

Think about buying a car. A functional requirement is that the car has airbags. An assurance requirement is that the car passed an independent crash test. The first describes what the feature does. The second tells you why you can believe it.

A useful habit is to write requirements so that they can be tested. The sentence, the system must be secure, cannot be tested. The sentence, all customer data must be encrypted when stored, can be tested.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital is buying a system to hold patient records. Health law says patient data must be protected. A risk assessment shows that stolen laptops are a major concern. The business needs doctors to reach records at the bedside. These facts become requirements: encrypt the data on every device, log every access, and make sure doctors can sign in within a few seconds.

The manager's mindset here is important. Security exists to support the business, so the controls have to fit how the business works.

Here is what to take away. Start from requirements, separate what a control does from how sure we are that it works, and write requirements that can be tested.

studyNotes.heading: Baselines, scoping, tailoring and cost
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the sensible order for choosing controls, using a worked example.

A good order of work is as follows.

- Identify the data, and how much harm a loss would cause.
- Assess the risks.
- Write the security requirements.
- Pick a baseline, which is a standard starting set of controls.
- Scope it by removing controls that do not apply.
- Tailor it by adjusting the rest to fit.
- Compare cost with benefit.
- Get management approval.

Think about a recipe. The baseline is the recipe as written. Scoping is crossing out the part about nuts, because nobody in your house eats nuts. Tailoring is adjusting the amount of salt to your family's taste.

For a government system in the United States, the baseline often comes from NIST, the National Institute of Standards and Technology. Its Special Publication 800-53 lists controls, and a companion publication, 800-53B, offers low, moderate and high baselines. The level is chosen by asking how much harm a loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability would cause. Other organizations start from ISO 27001, an international standard for managing information security. ISO stands for the International Organization for Standardization.

Here is the worked example. A company builds a website for staff holidays. It holds names and dates. A loss would cause moderate harm.

Step one. The team starts from a moderate baseline.

Step two, scoping. The baseline includes controls for wireless networks. The application has no wireless parts, so those controls are removed.

Step three, tailoring. The baseline says lock accounts after a stated number of failed logins. The team sets that number to five, to fit company policy.

Step four, a compensating control. The application cannot support a particular logging feature. So the team sends its records to a central logging service. A compensating control is an alternative that gives similar protection.

Step five, cost. A control should not cost more than the value it protects. A control worth 2,000 dollars a year should not guard an asset that could only lose 500 dollars a year.

Step six. Management reviews the result and signs its approval.

Write down every decision and the reason for it. An auditor will want to know why a control was removed.

Here is your takeaway. Start with a baseline, scope out what does not apply, tailor the rest, and let management decide.

studyNotes.heading: Common Criteria and its three key terms
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at how a product can be tested independently. The main international scheme is called Common Criteria.

Common Criteria, or CC, is an international standard for evaluating security products. It is published by ISO as standard 15408. Before it existed, each country had its own scheme, and a vendor might have to pay for the same test several times. Under Common Criteria, a product tested in one member country can be recognised in other member countries, usually up to a certain level.

There are three terms to learn.

- Protection Profile, or PP: what a type of customer needs. It is the shopping list.
- Security Target, or ST: what the vendor claims this product does.
- Target of Evaluation, or TOE: the exact product and setup being tested.

An everyday picture helps here. Suppose a town council wants safe child car seats. The council publishes a list of what every seat must do. That is the Protection Profile. A manufacturer says, our seat does all of this, and also has a special side bar. That is the Security Target. The exact model of seat, fitted in the exact way described, is the Target of Evaluation. An independent laboratory then tests it.

The flow is simple. Customers state their needs in a Protection Profile. The vendor writes a Security Target. An independent laboratory tests the Target of Evaluation against the claims. The national scheme then issues a certificate.

A Protection Profile is general and can apply to many products. A Security Target is specific to one product.

Here is a workplace example. A government wants firewalls for its offices. A published Protection Profile for network devices describes what such a device must do. A vendor writes a Security Target claiming that its firewall meets that profile. The laboratory tests version 9 of the firewall, in the configuration described. A later version is a different Target of Evaluation until it has been tested too.

Common Criteria replaced older schemes. The older United States scheme was the Trusted Computer System Evaluation Criteria, nicknamed the Orange Book. The older European scheme was the Information Technology Security Evaluation Criteria, or ITSEC. You only need to recognise those names.

Here is what to take away. The Protection Profile is the need, the Security Target is the claim, and the Target of Evaluation is the exact thing tested.

studyNotes.heading: Evaluation Assurance Levels in order
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to learn the seven Evaluation Assurance Levels, in their exact order.

An Evaluation Assurance Level, or EAL, tells you how deeply a product was examined. Here is the order.

- EAL1: functionally tested.
- EAL2: structurally tested.
- EAL3: methodically tested and checked.
- EAL4: methodically designed, tested and reviewed.
- EAL5: semi-formally designed and tested.
- EAL6: semi-formally verified design and tested.
- EAL7: formally verified design and tested.

Notice the pattern in the words. Levels one and two are about testing. Levels three and four add method. Levels five and six add semi-formal work, which means structured methods that fall short of full proof. Level seven adds formal work, which means mathematical proof.

Think about checking a new bridge. At the lowest level, you drive a car over it and see that it holds up. At the next level, you also look at the drawings of its structure. At the middle levels, engineers check that it was designed and built by a careful method. At the highest level, the design has been proved mathematically.

Let us walk through what each one is suited to. EAL1 suits a product where some confidence is wanted, but threats are not serious. EAL2 suits a product where the developer can give limited help to the tester. EAL3 suits moderate needs, with care taken during development. EAL4 is an important one for the exam. It is generally the highest level at which it makes economic sense to test an existing product that was not specially built for evaluation. Levels five, six and seven usually require that the product was designed from the beginning with the evaluation in mind. Those higher levels are used in places such as military and intelligence systems.

Here is a workplace example. A bank buys a commercial firewall rated EAL4. That is a sensible level for a product made for ordinary sale. A defence agency needs a device to separate networks of different classification. It may ask for a product rated EAL6 or above, built from the start for that purpose, and it will pay much more for it.

Here is your takeaway. Learn the seven names in order, and remember that semi-formal comes before formal, and that EAL7 means the design was formally verified.

studyNotes.heading: What a rating does not tell you
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the limits of a rating, because the exam enjoys testing them.

Here is the main trap. A higher Evaluation Assurance Level means more assurance, and not more security features. An EAL6 product may do less than an EAL4 product. A rating tells you how carefully the claims were examined, and not how impressive the claims were.

Think of a restaurant inspection. A very thorough inspection of a small sandwich shop tells you that the shop is clean. It does not tell you that the shop serves a better meal than the restaurant across the road.

There are other limits as well.

The rating covers only the configuration that was tested. If you turn on a feature that was not part of the test, or apply a new version, the rating may no longer apply.

The rating applies to the stated claims. So you must read the Security Target, and check that the Protection Profile matches your needs. A strong result against the wrong profile tells you very little.

A rating does not mean a product is free of flaws. New weaknesses are found after products have been tested.

Two more words matter here. Certification is the technical evaluation of a system. Authorization, which was once called accreditation, is when a senior manager formally accepts the risk and approves use. A laboratory or an assessor can certify. Only management can accept the risk. The person who signs is sometimes called the authorizing official.

This order is tested, so hold it firmly. First comes the technical evaluation, and then comes the management decision.

Here is a workplace example. A city council wants a database for housing benefit. A vendor offers an EAL5 product, and points proudly at the rating. The council's security manager reads the Security Target. It turns out that the tested configuration has no network connections at all. The council needs one with network connections, so the rating does not describe what the council would really be running. The manager asks for evidence that fits the real setup.

Testing by itself never replaces your own requirements. Ask whether the product solves your problem, in your setting, at a fair cost.

Here is what to take away. A rating measures depth of testing against stated claims, for one exact setup, and the final decision to accept risk always belongs to management.

studyNotes.heading: Other kinds of assurance and a worked decision
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at other kinds of evidence you can use, and then walk through a full buying decision.

Common Criteria is not the only source of assurance. Assurance simply means reasons to be confident.

For cryptographic hardware and software, the United States and Canada use FIPS 140. FIPS stands for Federal Information Processing Standard. The current version is FIPS 140-3. It has four levels, numbered one to four, and they go up in strength, with level four being the highest. At the higher levels, the module must show evidence of tampering, and then actively resist it.

For service providers, you can ask for independent audit reports. A common one is the SOC 2 report. SOC stands for System and Organization Controls. It describes how well a provider's controls are designed and, in a Type 2 report, how well they worked over a period of time. You may also ask for an ISO 27001 certificate, which shows that an organization runs a proper security management system.

You can also run your own tests, such as a trial in your own environment, a vulnerability scan or a penetration test, which is an authorized simulated attack.

Think about buying a used car. The maker's brochure is a claim. An official inspection certificate is independent evidence. A mechanic you hired yourself is your own test. The more you rely on the car, the more of these you want.

Here is a worked decision. A water company needs a device to connect a control network to its office network.

First, write the requirements. Only one kind of traffic may pass. Operators must log in individually. All activity must be logged. The device must be supportable for ten years.

Second, gather evidence. Product A has a higher rating, but against a profile for a different kind of device. Product B has a lower rating, against a profile that matches this use.

Third, check that the tested configuration is the one the company will run.

Fourth, weigh the cost, including staff time and support.

Fifth, ask a senior manager to accept the remaining risk. Product B is the better choice.

Here is your takeaway. Match the evidence to the need, use the assurance that fits the product, and let requirements lead the decision from start to finish.

How much confidence we need that it works.

International product evaluation standard, ISO/IEC 15408.
The security needs of a type of customer.
The vendor's security claims for its product.
The exact product and setup being tested.
Evaluation Assurance Level: 1 to 7, showing how deeply a product was tested.
A senior manager formally accepts the risk and approves use.

A Protection Profile is the need; a Security Target is the claim.

topics.memoryHook: PP is the Purchaser's list, ST is the Seller's promise, TOE is the Thing On the Examination table.

question.prompt: A government agency must buy a firewall. Product A is rated EAL6 against a profile written for small home-office devices. Product B is rated EAL4 against a profile that closely matches the agency's network needs. What should the agency do?
options: Buy Product A, as a higher level always means stronger security
Buy Product B, as lower-rated products cost less to run each year
Reject both products and demand an EAL7 rating for every firewall
Prefer Product B, as its evaluation fits the agency's needs
question.explanation: An EAL shows how deeply a product was tested against certain claims. Product B was tested against the agency's kind of need. Product A is tempting, but a high rating against the wrong profile says little about this network.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A project team states that a new application must lock an account after five failed logins, and also that an independent laboratory must confirm this feature works. How are these two statements BEST classified?
options: Both are functional requirements
Functional, then assurance
Assurance, then functional
Both are assurance requirements
practiceQuestions.explanation: The first says what the control must do, and the second says how confident we must be. Both are functional is tempting because both sound like rules, but independent confirmation is about confidence and not about behaviour.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company adopts a standard moderate control baseline for a new internal application. The application has no wireless components, so the team removes the wireless controls. What is this activity called?
options: Scoping
Tailoring
Certification
Compensating
practiceQuestions.explanation: Removing controls that do not apply is scoping. Tailoring is tempting because it also changes the baseline, but tailoring means adjusting the remaining controls to fit.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A sales director asks the security manager to buy a popular endpoint product because a competitor has just bought it. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Arrange a free trial of the product on several laptops
Ask the competitor how well the product has worked
Confirm the budget and request a quote from the vendor
Establish the security requirements the product must meet
practiceQuestions.explanation: Controls are selected to meet requirements, so the requirements come first. A trial is tempting because it is practical, but without requirements there is nothing to measure the trial against.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In a Common Criteria evaluation, which document states what a vendor claims its particular product does?
options: Protection Profile
Target of Evaluation
Security Target
Evaluation Assurance Level
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Security Target holds the vendor's claims for its product. The Protection Profile is tempting, but it states the needs of a type of customer and is not specific to one product.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which Evaluation Assurance Level is described as methodically designed, tested and reviewed?
options: EAL2
EAL3
EAL4
EAL5
practiceQuestions.explanation: EAL4 is methodically designed, tested and reviewed. EAL3 is tempting because it is also methodical, but it is methodically tested and checked, without the design work.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which sequence places Evaluation Assurance Level descriptions in order from LOWEST to HIGHEST?
options: Structurally tested, functionally tested, semi-formally designed and tested
Formally verified design and tested, semi-formally designed and tested, methodically tested and checked
Functionally tested, structurally tested, methodically tested and checked
Methodically tested and checked, functionally tested, formally verified design and tested
practiceQuestions.explanation: The levels begin with functionally tested, then structurally tested, then methodically tested and checked. The first option is tempting, but it reverses the two lowest levels.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A product has a Common Criteria rating for one tested setup. An administrator enables an extra remote feature that was not part of that setup. What is the MOST accurate statement?
options: The rating may no longer describe this setup
The rating stays valid until the certificate ends
The rating now applies at one level lower
The rating covers all features of that version
practiceQuestions.explanation: A rating applies only to the configuration that was evaluated. The fourth option is tempting because the product version is the same, but the Target of Evaluation is an exact setup and not just a version.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An independent assessor finishes a technical evaluation of a new system and reports several remaining risks. Who should decide whether the system may go into use?
options: The independent assessor who carried out the work
A senior official with authority over the risk
The lead developer who best understands the design
The vendor's accredited support engineer
practiceQuestions.explanation: Authorization is a management decision to accept risk. The assessor is tempting because the assessor knows the details, but certification is technical work and does not accept risk on the business's behalf.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A manager is comparing two firewalls. One is rated EAL5 and the other is rated EAL4. A colleague says the EAL5 product must have more security features. What is the BEST reply?
options: That is right, because each level adds further required features
That is right, because higher levels also need stronger algorithms
That is wrong, because a lower number means a higher rating
That is wrong, because the level measures depth of testing
practiceQuestions.explanation: A higher level means deeper evaluation, not more features. The first option is tempting because it sounds logical, but features are set by the Security Target and not by the level.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company wants confidence in a hardware device that performs encryption, and the buyer is specifically asking how strongly the device resists physical tampering. Which standard is MOST relevant?
options: FIPS 140
NIST Special Publication 800-53
A SOC 2 Type 2 report
practiceQuestions.explanation: FIPS 140 evaluates cryptographic modules, and its higher levels address tamper evidence and resistance. ISO 27001 is tempting because it is widely trusted, but it covers how an organization manages security, not the strength of a device.

topics.name: Security capabilities of information systems
topics.simpleExplanation: Computers have safety features built into them. Memory protection stops one program from reading another program's space, like walls between flats. A Trusted Platform Module is a small chip that guards keys inside one computer. A Hardware Security Module is a stronger, separate device that makes and guards many keys. Encryption scrambles data. Secure enclaves protect data while it is being used. All the parts that must be trusted together are called the trusted computing base.

studyNotes.heading: The trusted computing base
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at the idea of a trusted computing base. It is the foundation of everything else in this topic.

The Trusted Computing Base, or TCB, is all the hardware, firmware and software that enforce security on a system. Firmware is the low-level software stored on a chip. If the Trusted Computing Base fails, the whole security promise fails.

Think about the people you trust to run your home. Perhaps you trust the person who holds the master key, the company that installed the alarm, and the neighbour who watches the house. Those people are your trusted base. If one of them betrays you, your other protections do not help much. So you want that group to be as small as possible, and you want to check them carefully.

The same is true of computers. The Trusted Computing Base should be small, because small things can be tested fully. A large one will contain more mistakes.

There are two more terms that go with this idea.

The security perimeter is an imaginary line between the Trusted Computing Base and everything else. Anything inside the line is trusted. Anything outside it is not. When a program outside the line needs something from inside, it has to cross through a controlled interface.

A trusted path is a protected route between the user and the Trusted Computing Base. It makes sure that a fake login screen cannot steal a password. Many people remember the old Windows habit of pressing Control, Alt and Delete together before logging in. That key combination was handled by the operating system itself, so an ordinary program could not imitate it.

Here is a workplace example. A company runs a server that holds payroll data. The processor, the operating system's core, the login components and the access control software are part of the Trusted Computing Base. The word processor on a staff desktop is not. So the security team spends its effort on hardening the small trusted part, and it treats everything else as untrustworthy.

A good manager asks of any new product, does this need to be part of what we trust? Every trusted item adds risk.

Here is what to take away. The Trusted Computing Base is everything that enforces security, it should be as small as possible, and a trusted path protects the user's route into it.

studyNotes.heading: The reference monitor and the security kernel
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to look at the guard at the centre of a secure system, which is called the reference monitor.

A reference monitor is the idea of a guard that checks every access by a subject to an object. Remember that a subject is an active thing, such as a person or a program, and an object is a passive thing, such as a file.

Picture a nightclub with one door and one very strict doorkeeper. Every person who goes in is checked. There is no back door. Nobody can bribe the doorkeeper, or swap the doorkeeper for a friend. And the doorkeeper's rule book is short enough for the owner to read in a single sitting.

A reference monitor must have three qualities. You need to know them as a set.

- Tamperproof: nobody can change it.
- Always invoked: it cannot be bypassed.
- Verifiable: it is small enough to test completely.

The security kernel is the real thing that carries out the reference monitor idea. It is the actual hardware, firmware and software that make the checks. So the reference monitor is the concept, and the security kernel is the working implementation. If an exam question says concept, think of the reference monitor. If it says the actual components, think of the security kernel.

This connects back to our earlier topic on security models. A model says what the rules are. The reference monitor is the mechanism that applies those rules at every access. So if Bell-LaPadula says no read up, the reference monitor is what actually refuses the request.

Here is a workplace example. A government system stores files at several classification levels. When an analyst's program asks to open a file, the request goes to the security kernel. The kernel compares the analyst's clearance with the file's label. It refuses the request if the rules are broken, and it writes the attempt in an audit log. Because every request travels through this one point, the agency can be confident that nothing slips past.

There is a design lesson here. If any route to the data avoids the check, then the promise is broken.

Here is your takeaway. A reference monitor is the concept of a complete check on every access, and the security kernel is the real implementation. Learn the three qualities: tamperproof, always invoked and verifiable.

studyNotes.heading: Memory protection, process isolation and rings
studyNotes.body:
Next, we are going to look at memory protection, which keeps programs out of each other's way.

Memory is where a computer holds what it is working on. Many programs share the same memory chips at the same time. Without protection, one program could read or change what another program is holding. A bad program could read passwords held by your web browser.

Think of a block of flats. Everyone lives in the same building, and yet each flat has its own walls and its own door. Memory protection gives each program its own flat.

This is called process isolation. A process is simply a running program. The operating system and the processor work together to keep each process inside its own space. If a process tries to reach outside it, the attempt is stopped.

A technique that helps is called virtual memory addressing. Each program believes it has its own private set of addresses. The hardware quietly translates these to real locations. A program simply has no way of naming memory that belongs to another program.

Protection rings separate levels of power. You can picture a castle, with the most important people in the very centre. There are four rings, numbered from zero to three.

- Ring 0: the kernel, which is the core of the operating system. It has the most power.
- Ring 1 and Ring 2: often used for drivers and services, the parts that talk to hardware.
- Ring 3: normal applications, with the least power.

A lower number means more power. Many modern systems use only Ring 0 and Ring 3. Those two are often called kernel mode, or supervisor mode, and user mode.

A program in Ring 3 must ask the operating system to do privileged work. It makes what is called a system call. Think of a hotel guest. The guest cannot walk into the kitchen and cook. The guest rings room service, and the staff do the work.

Here is a workplace example. A staff member's spreadsheet program has a flaw, and an attacker exploits it. Because the program runs in user mode, the attacker has the power of that program only. To take over the machine, the attacker would need a second flaw to break into kernel mode.

Here is what to take away. Process isolation keeps each program in its own space, and a lower ring number means more power.

studyNotes.heading: Buffer overflows, ASLR and DEP
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to look at a classic attack on memory, and at two features that help to stop it.

A buffer is a block of memory set aside to hold something, such as a name typed into a form. A buffer overflow happens when a program writes more data into a buffer than it can hold, so that the extra data spills into nearby memory.

Imagine pouring a litre of water into a small glass standing on a kitchen counter. The water does not vanish. It spills over and soaks the letters lying next to the glass. In memory, the spilled data can overwrite important values, including the address that tells the processor where to go next. An attacker who controls that address can steer the program into running the attacker's own instructions.

The true fix is writing careful code that checks the length of the input before storing it. But two operating system features give extra protection, in case a mistake gets through.

The first is ASLR, which stands for Address Space Layout Randomization. It places parts of a program at random memory addresses each time the program starts. So an attacker cannot predict where to jump. Think of a shop that rearranges its shelves each morning. A thief who memorised last week's layout will be lost.

The second is DEP, which stands for Data Execution Prevention. It marks areas of memory as being for data only, so that code cannot run from them. It is like a rule that a storage room may hold boxes, but nobody may work in it. Even if an attacker gets instructions into the storage room, those instructions cannot be carried out.

One hides the target, and the other refuses to run code in data areas. Neither is perfect, which is another example of defense in depth.

Here is a workplace example. A company has an older web application with a known buffer overflow. While the application is being replaced, the security manager makes sure that it runs on an operating system with both features switched on, and with a firewall limiting who can reach it. These are compensating controls. The real fix is still to correct the code.

Here is your takeaway. Buffer overflows spill data into nearby memory, ASLR randomizes where things are, DEP stops code running from data areas, and careful code is the true fix.

studyNotes.heading: TPM and HSM
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at two pieces of hardware that protect keys. The exam likes to ask you to tell them apart.

A Trusted Platform Module, or TPM, is a chip on one computer's main board. It stores keys safely, and it measures the boot process. To measure means to take a fingerprint of each piece of startup code, one after another, and to record those fingerprints inside the chip. If someone tampers with startup files, the fingerprints change.

The chip can be told to release a key only if the fingerprints match the expected values. This is called sealing. So if someone tampers with the startup files, the Trusted Platform Module can refuse to release the disk encryption key. Think of a safe bolted inside your own house, which opens only if the house looks exactly as it did when you left. This is how a stolen laptop stays protected. Microsoft BitLocker, which encrypts Windows disks, commonly uses this feature.

A Hardware Security Module, or HSM, is a hardened device, often a plug-in card or a network box. It is built to resist tampering. It creates, stores and uses many keys, and it does encryption work quickly. Keys are not meant to leave it. Applications send data in to be signed or decrypted, and they receive only the answer.

Banks use them. So do certificate authorities, which issue digital identity documents. Many are tested under FIPS 140, a United States government standard for cryptographic modules. FIPS stands for Federal Information Processing Standard.

To tell them apart, remember these points.

- Trusted Platform Module: one device, cheap and built in.
- Hardware Security Module: many keys, high volume, tamper resistant and costly.

Here is a workplace example of each. A company issues laptops to staff. It uses each laptop's Trusted Platform Module to bind the disk encryption key to that laptop. Separately, the company runs a payment platform that signs thousands of transactions each second. That platform uses a pair of Hardware Security Modules, so that the signing keys are never exposed in ordinary server memory.

If you are asked which one fits a scenario, ask how many keys are involved, how much work is being done, and whether it serves one device or many.

Here is what to take away. A Trusted Platform Module protects one machine and checks its startup. A Hardware Security Module serves many keys at scale.

studyNotes.heading: Encryption and secure enclaves
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we are going to look at encryption as a system capability, and at secure enclaves.

Encryption turns readable data into scrambled data that needs a key to read. Decryption turns it back. We will study how it works in later topics. Here, we need to understand that systems protect data in different ways, depending on where the data is. Data has three states.

- At rest: stored on a disk. Use disk or database encryption.
- In transit: moving over a network. Use TLS, or Transport Layer Security, the protection behind the padlock in a web browser.
- In use: being worked on in memory. This is the hardest state to protect.

Here is an everyday picture. A letter in a locked drawer is at rest. A letter in a sealed envelope in the post is in transit. A letter open on your desk while you read it is in use. Anyone looking over your shoulder can see it.

The reason that data in use is so hard to protect is that the processor generally needs the data in readable form in order to work on it.

Modern processors often include special instructions that make encryption much faster, so that encrypting everything is no longer a heavy burden on the system.

A secure enclave, also called a Trusted Execution Environment, is a walled-off part of the processor. Code and data inside are protected even from the operating system. So even if an attacker controls the operating system, the contents of the enclave stay hidden. Intel SGX and Arm TrustZone are examples. Phones use enclaves to protect fingerprint data. Using enclaves to protect data while it is being processed is often called confidential computing.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital wants to analyse patient records on a cloud provider's servers, but it does not want the provider's staff to be able to see them. The data travels with Transport Layer Security. It is encrypted when stored. And it is processed inside a secure enclave, so that it remains protected in use. All three states have now been covered.

No single feature is enough, so a manager should combine them according to risk.

Here is your takeaway. Protect data at rest, in transit and in use, and remember that enclaves shield data while it is being worked on.

Concept of a guard that checks every access.
The actual parts that implement the reference monitor.
Keeping each running program in its own memory space.
Levels of power; Ring 0 is highest, Ring 3 is for applications.
Address Space Layout Randomization: randomizes memory locations to frustrate attackers.
Data Execution Prevention: stops code from running in data areas.
Trusted Platform Module: a chip that guards keys and checks startup on one device.
Hardware Security Module: a hardened device that makes, stores and uses many keys.
A protected part of the processor that shields data while in use.

keyPoints: The TCB should be as small as possible.
A reference monitor is tamperproof, always invoked and verifiable.
