That is why AES with a 256-bit key is considered safe enough, and why the answer to quantum threats on symmetric keys is simply a longer key.

Post-quantum cryptography means new methods designed to resist quantum attacks, and it runs on ordinary computers. Do not confuse it with quantum key distribution, which uses physics to share keys over special equipment.

NIST, the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology, published its first post-quantum standards in 2024. Learn these names.

- ML-KEM: for key exchange, in the standard called FIPS 203.
- ML-DSA: for digital signatures, in FIPS 204.
- SLH-DSA: also for signatures, in FIPS 205.

FIPS stands for Federal Information Processing Standard.

There is one more threat to understand, known as harvest now, decrypt later. An attacker can record encrypted traffic today, and store it until a quantum computer becomes available. Data that needs to stay secret for many years is therefore at risk already.

Here is a workplace example. A government agency holds records that must remain secret for fifty years. It starts now by listing everywhere it uses public key cryptography. It then plans a move to post-quantum methods, starting with the data that must stay secret the longest. This ability to switch methods easily is called crypto agility.

A wise manager keeps that list up to date, and does not wait for an emergency.

Here is your takeaway. Shor's algorithm threatens public key methods, Grover's algorithm halves symmetric strength, and planning for the change should begin now.

studyNotes.heading: Hashing and HMAC
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to look at hashing, which is different from encryption.

A hash function turns data of any size into a short fixed-size value. That value is called a hash, or a digest. It is one-way, so you cannot turn it back into the original. Any small change to the input gives a very different result.

Think of a fingerprint. Your fingerprint identifies you, and it is much smaller than you are. But nobody can rebuild you from your fingerprint.

Hashing supports integrity. It does not provide confidentiality, because nothing is hidden, and there is no key.

A collision is when two inputs give the same hash. A good hash function makes collisions extremely hard to find. Here are the sizes to know.

- MD5, or Message Digest 5: 128 bits. Broken.
- SHA-1, or Secure Hash Algorithm 1: 160 bits. Broken.
- SHA-2: includes 224, 256, 384 and 512-bit versions. In wide use.
- SHA-3: a newer design with the same output sizes.

Hashes are also used to store passwords. A system keeps the hash, and not the password. A salt is a random value added before hashing, so that two people with the same password end up with different hashes. For passwords, deliberately slow methods are best, such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2.

Now to HMAC, which stands for Hash-based Message Authentication Code. It mixes a shared secret key into the hash. It proves integrity, and it proves that the sender holds the key.

Think of two friends who agree on a secret word. When sending a note, the writer adds the secret word before calculating a checksum. Someone who alters the note cannot produce the right checksum without the word.

HMAC cannot give non-repudiation, because both sides hold the same key. Either side could have created it.

Here is a workplace example. A software company publishes a hash next to each download. A customer checks that the hash matches. That detects accidental damage. But an attacker who could change the download could also change the hash on the same web page. So on its own, a hash does not prove who published it. That takes a digital signature.

Here is what to take away. A hash is a one-way fingerprint for integrity, and HMAC adds a shared secret key, but it cannot give non-repudiation.

studyNotes.heading: How a digital signature works
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we are going to walk through a digital signature step by step, noting which key does what.

A digital signature proves who sent a message, and that it was not changed. It joins together the two ideas we have just learned, which are hashing and asymmetric keys.

Ana is signing a contract for Ben. Here are the steps.

- Step 1: Ana hashes the contract.
- Step 2: Ana encrypts the hash with her private key. This is the signature.
- Step 3: Ana sends the contract and the signature.
- Step 4: Ben decrypts the signature with Ana's public key, which reveals her hash.
- Step 5: Ben hashes the contract himself.
- Step 6: Ben compares the two hashes. A match proves the signature is good.

Think about why this works. Only Ana holds her private key, so only Ana could have made that signature. That gives authentication and non-repudiation. If even one comma in the contract had changed, Ben's hash would be different. That gives integrity.

So a signature gives integrity, authentication and non-repudiation. It does not give confidentiality, because the contract itself is not encrypted. Anybody can read it.

To add secrecy, Ana would also encrypt the signed message with Ben's public key. Then two different key pairs are in use. Ana's private key signs. Ben's public key encrypts.

A small point of accuracy. Encrypting the hash is the traditional way of teaching this, and it is the way the exam tends to describe it. Some algorithms, such as DSA, create a signature in a different mathematical way, but the idea of private key to sign and public key to verify is the same.

Why do we sign the hash and not the whole document? Because the hash is short, and asymmetric work is slow. Signing a short hash takes very little time.

Here is a workplace example. A software company signs its update files with its private key. Every customer's computer holds the company's public key, and it checks each update before installing it. An attacker who alters an update cannot create a valid signature without the private key, so the update is refused.

Here is your takeaway. Sign with the sender's private key, verify with the sender's public key, and remember that a signature gives integrity, authentication and non-repudiation, but not secrecy.

keyTerms.meaning: Uses a public and private key pair.
Asymmetric method based on factoring very large numbers.
Elliptic Curve Cryptography: strong security with small keys.
A way for two parties to agree a shared secret over an open network.
A key stolen later cannot unlock earlier sessions.
A fixed-size, one-way fingerprint of data.
Two different inputs that produce the same hash.
Hash-based Message Authentication Code: a hash mixed with a shared secret key.
A hash encrypted with the sender's private key.
The sender cannot later deny sending it.

keyPoints: Secrecy uses the receiver's public key; signing uses the sender's private key.
Real systems use asymmetric keys to share a symmetric key.
Diffie-Hellman agrees a key but does not prove identity alone.
HMAC proves integrity and authenticity, but not non-repudiation.
Signatures give integrity, authentication and non-repudiation, not secrecy.
topics.memoryHook: Lock a secret with THEIR public key. Sign with YOUR private key.

question.prompt: A supplier must send a purchase contract to a customer. The customer needs proof that the supplier sent it and that it was not altered, and the supplier must not be able to deny sending it. The contract itself is not secret. What should the supplier do?
options: Encrypt the contract with the customer's public key
Hash the contract and sign the hash with its private key
Send the contract with an HMAC using a shared secret key
Encrypt the contract with its own symmetric session key
question.explanation: Only a digital signature made with the sender's private key gives non-repudiation. HMAC is tempting because it shows integrity, but both sides hold the key, so either could have created it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Lena must send a confidential file so that only Omar can read it. Which key should encrypt it?
options: Lena's private key
Lena's public key
Omar's private key
Omar's public key
practiceQuestions.explanation: Encrypting with the receiver's public key means only the receiver's private key can open it. Lena's private key is tempting, but that is used for signing, and anyone with her public key could read the result.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which key does a signer use to create a digital signature, and which key does the receiver use to check it?
options: Signer's private key, then signer's public key
Receiver's public key, then receiver's private key
Signer's public key, then signer's private key
Receiver's private key, then signer's public key
practiceQuestions.explanation: The signer uses its own private key, and anyone can verify using the signer's public key. Receiver's public key is tempting, but that pair is used for secrecy and proves nothing about who sent the message.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company is building a battery-powered sensor that must sign its readings. The signing method must be strong but use as little power as possible. Which choice is BEST?
options: RSA with a 4096-bit key
A 256-bit elliptic curve key
HMAC with a key shared by all sensors
MD5 applied to each reading
practiceQuestions.explanation: Elliptic curves give strong signatures with small keys and little power. HMAC is tempting because it is light, but a shared key cannot prove which sensor signed a reading.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two systems use plain Diffie-Hellman to agree on a shared key over the internet, with no other checks. What is the MAIN weakness of this setup?
options: The key they agree cannot be used with AES
The exchange sends the shared secret openly
Neither side can prove who the other really is
The method needs a separate one-time pad
practiceQuestions.explanation: Without authentication, an attacker can sit in the middle and agree a key with each side. Sending the secret openly is tempting, but the point of Diffie-Hellman is that the shared secret never travels across the network.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An attacker recorded a company's encrypted web traffic last year, and has now stolen the server's private key. The company used ephemeral Diffie-Hellman for every session. What is the MOST likely result?
options: All of last year's traffic can now be read at once
Only traffic from the most recent week can be read
Last year's traffic stays protected by forward secrecy
The server's certificate becomes readable to the attacker
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ephemeral exchanges use new values each session, so a stolen long-term key does not unlock past sessions. The first option is tempting, and it would be true if the server's key had been used to encrypt session keys directly.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A large quantum computer becomes available. Which of the following is the MOST seriously threatened?
options: AES with a 256-bit key
RSA with a 3072-bit key
SHA-3 with a 512-bit output
A properly used one-time pad
practiceQuestions.explanation: Shor's algorithm would break RSA regardless of practical key length. AES with a 256-bit key is tempting because it is widely used, but Grover's algorithm only halves its strength, which leaves it strong.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A file server stores hashes of its documents and compares them each night. What does this MOSTLY provide?
options: Confidentiality of the documents
Non-repudiation by the authors
Availability of the file server
Detection of unauthorized changes
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hashes support integrity, so a change shows up as a mismatch. Confidentiality is tempting because hashing can look like encryption, but hashing hides nothing in the documents themselves.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two banks use HMAC with a shared key to protect messages between them. One bank later denies having sent a particular message. Why can the other bank NOT prove that it did?
options: Either bank holding the key could have made the code
HMAC cannot detect whether a message has been changed
HMAC does not use any type of cryptographic key
HMAC can be calculated only by a third party
practiceQuestions.explanation: Both banks hold the same key, so neither can prove the other made it, and there is no non-repudiation. The second option is tempting, but HMAC does detect changes. That is integrity, and it is what HMAC does well.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A contract is sent with a digital signature, but it is not encrypted. Which security goal is NOT achieved?
options: Integrity
Authentication
Non-repudiation
Confidentiality
practiceQuestions.explanation: A signature does not hide the contract, so anyone can read it. Non-repudiation is tempting if you are unsure, but a private key signature is exactly what provides it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company must transfer a confidential 200 gigabyte database to a partner over the internet, as quickly as possible, with the partner's identity assured. Which approach is BEST?
options: Encrypt the entire database using the partner's public RSA key
Agree a session key using certificates, and encrypt with AES
Hash the entire database, and post the hash on the website
Sign the database with the company's own private key
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hybrid encryption uses authenticated public key methods to set up a session key, and AES does the bulk work quickly. Using RSA on the whole database is tempting because it provides secrecy, but it is far too slow for large amounts of data.

topics.name: PKI and key management
topics.simpleExplanation: How do you know a public key really belongs to your bank? A trusted organization vouches for it, much like a government issues a passport. This system is called Public Key Infrastructure, or PKI. A digital certificate is the passport. A Certificate Authority is the passport office. Keys also need care throughout their lives. They must be created safely, stored safely, changed regularly and destroyed when finished. Most real failures happen because keys are poorly managed.

studyNotes.heading: Why we need PKI, and who does what
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at why we need something called Public Key Infrastructure, and at the roles within it.

Public key cryptography has a gap. How do you know that a public key really belongs to your bank? An attacker could publish a key and claim to be the bank. So someone trusted has to vouch for it.

Think of a passport. You trust a passport because you trust the government that issued it. You do not need to know the person. You only need to trust the office that checked them.

Public Key Infrastructure, or PKI, is the people, rules and systems that link public keys to identities. A digital certificate is the passport.

These are the parties.

- Certificate Authority, or CA: issues and signs certificates.
- Registration Authority, or RA: checks identity on behalf of the Certificate Authority. It does not issue certificates.
- Root CA: the top of the trust chain. It is often kept offline for safety.
- Intermediate CA: issues certificates under the root, so that the root stays protected.

Think of the passport office again. The Certificate Authority is the office that issues the passport. The Registration Authority is the clerk at the counter who checks your documents.

A chain of trust runs like this. Your computer trusts a small number of root certificates, which came installed with the operating system or browser. A root has signed an intermediate. The intermediate has signed the website's certificate. Your computer follows that chain back to the root.

If the root's private key were stolen, every certificate below it could no longer be trusted. That is why the root is kept offline and in a highly protected device, and why intermediates do the daily work.

Here is a workplace example. A company runs its own private Certificate Authority for internal systems. The root sits powered off in a safe, and it is used only to sign new intermediates. An intermediate issues certificates to staff laptops and servers. Human resources acts as the Registration Authority, confirming that each person really works there.

An alternative to a central authority is a web of trust, in which individuals vouch for one another. PGP, or Pretty Good Privacy, uses this approach.

Here is what to take away. The Certificate Authority issues certificates, the Registration Authority only checks identity, and the root is kept offline.

studyNotes.heading: Digital certificates and how to get one
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to look at what is inside a digital certificate, and at how someone gets one.

A digital certificate follows a standard called X.509. It contains the following.

- The owner's name, called the subject.
- The owner's public key.
- The issuer's name.
- A serial number and validity dates.
- The issuer's digital signature.

Look at a passport, and you find similar things. There is a name, a number, the dates it is valid for, and the mark of the issuing government. Notice what is missing from the list. The owner's private key is not in the certificate. It never is.

A certificate simply says this: the Certificate Authority declares that this public key belongs to this name, for this period of time.

Here are the steps to get a certificate.

- Step 1: Create a key pair. The private key stays with you.
- Step 2: Send a Certificate Signing Request, or CSR, containing your public key.
- Step 3: The Registration Authority or the Certificate Authority checks your identity.
- Step 4: The Certificate Authority signs and issues the certificate.

The important point is in Step 1. The private key does not leave you. You send the public key only. If a service offers to create your private key and email it to you, that should worry you.

Certificates come in different kinds. A wildcard certificate covers all of the names under a domain, such as every address ending in a company's name. It is convenient, but if its private key is stolen, every one of those sites is exposed. A certificate can also be used to identify a user or a device, and not only a website.

For web certificates there are three levels of identity checking. Domain validation only proves control of the web address. Organization validation also checks the organization. Extended validation checks more thoroughly.

Here is a workplace example. A company sets up a new web server. An administrator generates a key pair on the server, sends a signing request, proves control of the domain and installs the issued certificate. The private key never left the server.

Here is your takeaway. A certificate binds a public key to a name, and is signed by the issuer. The private key is never in the certificate and never leaves its owner.

studyNotes.heading: How a certificate is checked
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at what happens when your computer decides whether to trust a certificate.

Think about a guard at a border. The guard looks at your passport and asks a series of questions. Was this issued by a government we recognise? Has it expired? Does the photo match the person standing here? Is it on the list of stolen passports? Only if all of the answers are good are you let through.

A web browser does the same, and it checks these things.

- The issuer's signature is valid, and it links to a trusted root.
- Today's date is within the validity dates.
- The name matches the website.
- The certificate has not been revoked.

Let us walk through an example. Maria visits her bank's website. The web server sends its certificate, along with the intermediate certificate that signed it.

Maria's browser uses the intermediate's public key to check the signature on the bank's certificate. Then it uses the root's public key, which is already stored on her device, to check the signature on the intermediate's certificate. The chain is complete.

The browser checks the dates, and finds that the certificate is still valid. It checks that the name on the certificate matches the address she typed. It checks revocation, which we will look at next. Everything is fine, and the padlock appears.

Now change one fact. Suppose that an attacker sends a certificate with the bank's name on it, but issued by an authority the browser does not trust. The chain fails, and the browser warns Maria. If she clicks through the warning, she may be talking to an impostor. This is why staff should be trained not to dismiss certificate warnings.

A technique called certificate pinning goes one step further. An application remembers exactly which certificate or key to expect from a server, and refuses anything else. It defends against a wrongly issued certificate, but it can cause outages if certificates change and the application is not updated.

In the workplace, expired certificates are a very common cause of outages. A certificate expires quietly at midnight, and a major service stops working. A manager should insist on an inventory of certificates, with automatic reminders or automatic renewal.

Here is what to take away. A client checks the signature chain, the dates, the name and the revocation status, and an expired certificate is a preventable outage.

studyNotes.heading: Revocation: CRL and OCSP
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to look at how a certificate gets cancelled before its end date. This is called revocation, and the exam likes to compare the two main ways of checking it.

A common reason for revocation is a stolen private key. Others are that the owner has left the organization, or that the certificate was issued wrongly.

The first method is a Certificate Revocation List, or CRL. This is a signed list of the serial numbers of cancelled certificates, which the Certificate Authority publishes from time to time. Clients must download it. It can grow large and it can be out of date. Think of a printed list of stolen passports, sent out to border posts once a day. A passport stolen this morning will not appear on the list until tomorrow.

The second method is OCSP, the Online Certificate Status Protocol. It lets a client ask about one certificate and get an answer right away. The answer is one of good, revoked or unknown. Think of the guard telephoning the passport office about one passport.

Here is the comparison, spoken plainly.

A list is downloaded in full, and may be stale. A protocol request asks about a single certificate, and is current.

OCSP has its own drawbacks. The authority that answers learns which sites you are visiting, which raises a privacy concern. If the responder is down, some clients simply carry on, and that weakens the check.

OCSP stapling solves those problems. The web server itself regularly gets a recent signed answer, and it attaches that answer to its certificate when it talks to a client. This is faster and more private.

Now for the correct order of work. If a private key is stolen, revoke the certificate first, and then issue a new one with a new key pair. Do not reuse the old key, because it is exposed.

Here is a workplace example. A web administrator finds the company's private key on a public code sharing site. The security manager asks the Certificate Authority to revoke the certificate at once, then generates a new key pair, then finds out how the key was exposed.

Here is your takeaway. A Certificate Revocation List is a published list, OCSP is a live check on one certificate, and when a key is stolen, you revoke first.

studyNotes.heading: The key lifecycle and rotation
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to follow a key through its whole life. Most real cryptographic failures happen because keys are poorly managed.

Keys pass through these stages.

- Generation: make keys with strong random numbers.
- Distribution: move them safely.
- Storage: never keep them beside the data, and protect them in hardware when possible.
- Use: use each key for one purpose only.
- Rotation: replace keys on a schedule.
- Backup or archive: keep what is needed to read old data.
- Revocation: stop trusting a key that is exposed.
- Destruction: remove all copies when the key is no longer needed.

Think about the key to a business premises. It is cut by a locksmith you trust. It is handed over in person. It is kept on a secure key ring. It is used only for that door. The lock is changed from time to time. A spare is kept somewhere safe. If the key is lost, the lock is changed. And when the business moves out, every copy is handed back.

A key's allowed period of use is its cryptoperiod. Rotation means replacing a key before that period is over. Why bother? A key that has been used for a very long time has protected more data, so a single theft would expose more. Rotation limits the damage.

There is also a practical question. What happens to data that was encrypted with the old key? It has to be either re-encrypted with the new key, or the old key has to be retained to read it. A common approach is to encrypt data with one key and to protect that key with another, called a key encryption key. You can then rotate the outer key without re-encrypting all of the data. This is known as envelope encryption.

Destruction has a special use. If you destroy every copy of a key, the data it protected can never be read again. This is called cryptographic erasure, and it is very useful in the cloud, where you cannot physically destroy the provider's disks.

The cryptographic lifecycle also covers algorithms. Choose approved algorithms, track them, and replace them as they weaken. Set this out in policy.

Here is what to take away. Keys have a whole life, from generation to destruction, and a planned rotation limits how much a single stolen key can expose.

studyNotes.heading: Protecting and recovering keys
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we are going to look at how to make sure that keys can be recovered when needed, without trusting any one person too much.

Imagine that the one person who knows the combination to the company safe leaves suddenly. The contents are lost. Now imagine that person is dishonest. The contents are stolen. We need to protect against both of these situations.

Key escrow means a trusted third party holds a copy of a key, so that it can be recovered under agreed rules. A recovery agent is a person or account allowed to recover data, for example after an employee leaves.

No one person should control an important key alone. Three controls prevent this.

- Split knowledge: each person holds only part of a key.
- Dual control: two people must act together.
- M of N control: any M out of N people can recover the key.

These are similar, so let us separate them with an everyday picture. Split knowledge is each of two friends knowing half of the combination. Dual control is the bank's safe deposit box, where your key and the bank's key must be turned at the same time. M of N control is a club where any three of the five committee members can open the account together.

Here is a worked example. With 3 of 5 control, five managers hold pieces. Any three can recover the key. Two cannot, so one or two dishonest people cannot act alone. And if two managers are unavailable, the remaining three can still act, so one lost person does not stop the business.

A Hardware Security Module, or HSM, is a tamper-resistant device that protects keys. Use one for root Certificate Authority keys and other high-value keys. Operations on the root are often done in a formal key ceremony, where several trusted people attend, each carrying out set steps, and everything is recorded.

Here is a workplace example. A bank needs to protect its master encryption key. The key is stored in a Hardware Security Module. Activating it requires smart cards held by three of five named officers. Nobody can use the key alone, and nobody's resignation can lock the bank out.

Here is your takeaway. Recover keys through controlled escrow, and use split knowledge, dual control and M of N, so that no one person holds full power.

question.prompt: A company learns that the private key for its public website has been stolen. The certificate still has eight months before it expires. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Wait for the expiry date and then issue a certificate with a longer key
Change the website administrator's password and review the access logs
Copy the current private key to a Hardware Security Module for safety
Have the certificate revoked so that others will stop trusting the key
question.explanation: A stolen private key lets attackers pose as the company, so trust in it must be ended first by revoking the certificate. Changing passwords is tempting, but it leaves the stolen key valid. Afterward, issue a new certificate with a new key pair.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A staff member in human resources confirms that certificate applicants really work for the company, but does not sign any certificates. Which role is this person performing?
options: Certificate Authority
Root authority
Registration Authority
Intermediate authority
practiceQuestions.explanation: A Registration Authority checks identity and does not issue certificates. Certificate Authority is tempting because it is the better known term, but that is the party that actually signs.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company is setting up an internal certificate hierarchy. Which design BEST protects the root key?
options: Keep the root online so that it can issue certificates quickly
Keep the root offline and let intermediates issue certificates
Give every department a copy of the root's private key
Store the root's private key on the web server for backups
practiceQuestions.explanation: An offline root reduces exposure, and intermediates do the daily work. Keeping the root online is tempting for speed, but compromise of the root would destroy trust in everything beneath it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which item is NOT found in an X.509 digital certificate?
options: The owner's private key
The owner's public key
The issuer's signature
The validity dates
practiceQuestions.explanation: A private key is never placed in a certificate. The owner's public key is tempting if you confuse the two, but the public key is the very thing the certificate exists to vouch for.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A system administrator is requesting a certificate for a new server. Which action should be taken FIRST?
options: Install the certificate on the new server
Ask the Certificate Authority to issue a private key
Publish the new public key on the website
Generate a key pair on the server
practiceQuestions.explanation: The key pair comes first, and the public key is then sent in a signing request. Asking the authority for a private key is tempting, but the private key should be created by, and stay with, its owner.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A user receives a browser warning that a website's certificate was issued by an unknown authority. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The website's name has been shortened
The certificate's chain does not reach a trusted root
The website's public key is the wrong length
The server has stapled its status response
practiceQuestions.explanation: An unknown issuer means the chain cannot be followed back to a trusted root. Stapling is tempting as a technical sounding option, but stapling is a normal way of speeding up revocation checks.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A service must learn the current status of one certificate during a connection, with no need to download a large file. Which method is BEST?
options: Downloading a Certificate Revocation List
Checking the certificate's validity dates
The Online Certificate Status Protocol
Reading the certificate's subject name
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Online Certificate Status Protocol answers about one certificate right away. A Certificate Revocation List is tempting because it also deals with revocation, but it must be downloaded in full and may be out of date.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company wants revocation checks that are fast and do not reveal to the certificate authority which sites its users visit. Which technique BEST meets this need?
options: Certificate pinning
Wildcard certificates
A longer validity period
OCSP stapling
practiceQuestions.explanation: With stapling, the web server supplies a recent signed status, so clients need not contact the authority. Pinning is tempting because it strengthens checking, but it does not address revocation.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A database encrypted in a public cloud must be permanently and quickly made unreadable. The company cannot physically destroy the provider's disks. What is the BEST method?
options: Destroy every copy of the encryption key
Delete the database through the normal console
Ask the provider to confirm that the disks are full
Rename the database and restrict all access to it
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cryptographic erasure works because without the key the data can never be read. Normal deletion is tempting because it is simple, but it does not guarantee that the data is gone from the disks.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A master key is protected so that any four of seven executives can together restore it. Which control does this describe?
options: Key rotation
M of N control
Key wrapping
Certificate pinning
practiceQuestions.explanation: Any M out of N people together can recover the key, which here means four of seven. Key rotation is tempting because it is also a key management control, but it means replacing keys on a schedule.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A web server's private key has been exposed. The security manager has already had the certificate revoked. What should happen NEXT?
options: Reinstall the same certificate after changing the server password
Issue a certificate for the same key with a later end date
Generate a new key pair and obtain a new certificate
Wait for the next scheduled renewal before doing anything
practiceQuestions.explanation: The old key is exposed and must not be used again, so a new key pair is needed. Extending the certificate for the same key is tempting because it is quick, but the stolen key would remain valid for attackers.

topics.name: Cryptanalytic attacks
topics.simpleExplanation: Cryptanalysis means trying to break protection without having the key. Some attackers try every key. Some look for patterns in the scrambled text. Others ignore the mathematics and attack the way it was built, for example by timing how long a device takes to answer. Others steal a password's stored fingerprint and reuse it, or forge network passes. Ransomware turns encryption against you by locking your files for money. Good defense means good design, good keys and good backups.

studyNotes.heading: Attacks grouped by what the attacker holds
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at attacks on the mathematics of encryption. They are grouped by what the attacker has to work with.

Cryptanalysis means trying to break protection without having the key. Think of a locked diary. How you might attack it depends on what you can get hold of. A single page in code gives you little to go on. If you also have that page in plain words, you can compare the two.

Here are the main types.

- Brute force: try every possible key.
- Ciphertext only: the attacker has only scrambled text.
- Known plaintext: the attacker has some original text and its scrambled version.
- Chosen plaintext: the attacker chooses text to encrypt and studies the output.
- Chosen ciphertext: the attacker chooses scrambled text to decrypt and studies the output.

Ciphertext only is the hardest case for the attacker, because there is the least to work with. Chosen attacks are the most powerful, because the attacker can run experiments.

Let us work through brute force with some numbers. A key of 8 bits has 256 possible values. Each extra bit doubles that number. The Data Encryption Standard, or DES, has a 56-bit key, which gives two to the power of 56 possible keys. That is about 72 quadrillion. It sounds huge, but modern hardware can get through it. A 128-bit key has two to the power of 128 possible keys, and that is far beyond any practical search. So a long key makes brute force impractical.

Passwords are attacked in a similar way, often with a dictionary of likely words. A rainbow table is a large precomputed list of hashes, which are short fingerprints of data. A salt is a random value added to each password before hashing, and it makes such tables useless.

Here is a workplace example of known plaintext. Every email from a company ends with the same long footer. An attacker who knows that footer has a piece of known plaintext to compare against the encrypted message. Modern algorithms are designed to resist this. Older ones are not.

Here is what to take away. Attacks on the mathematics are named after what the attacker holds, ciphertext only is the hardest for the attacker, and long keys defeat brute force.

studyNotes.heading: Frequency analysis, birthdays and meeting in the middle
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at three more attacks on the mathematics, each one of which is well worth knowing by name.

Frequency analysis means counting how often letters appear. In English, the letter E is the most common, followed by T and A. If a message has been scrambled by swapping each letter for another, the most common symbol in the scrambled message probably stands for E. This defeats simple substitution ciphers, which swap each letter for another. Modern ciphers are not vulnerable to it, because good diffusion spreads every letter across the output.

The birthday attack looks for hash collisions. A hash is a short fingerprint of data, and a collision is two inputs with the same hash. The name comes from a surprising fact. In a room of only 23 people, there is slightly better than an even chance that two people share a birthday. That is because you are comparing every person with every other person, and not with one chosen date.

The same maths applies to hashes. For a hash of a given length, you expect to find a collision after trying about as many inputs as two raised to half of that length. So a 160-bit hash gives only about 80 bits of collision strength. A 256-bit hash gives about 128 bits. That is why short hashes such as MD5, or Message Digest 5, at 128 bits, are not safe. Forged signatures are the danger. If two different documents share a hash, a signature on one is valid for the other.

A meet-in-the-middle attack works from both ends of a double encryption. The attacker encrypts a known piece of text with every possible first key, and decrypts the ciphertext with every possible second key. Then the attacker looks for a match in the middle. It is the reason that Double DES, the idea of using DES twice with two keys, was never adopted.

Do not confuse meet in the middle with man in the middle. They sound alike. Meet in the middle is a mathematical attack on double encryption. Man in the middle is an attack on a live conversation, which we will come to soon.

Here is your takeaway. Frequency analysis breaks simple substitution, the birthday attack finds hash collisions at about half the bits, and meet in the middle is the reason Double DES failed.

studyNotes.heading: Attacks on how it was built
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to look at attacks that go around strong mathematics, by attacking how the system was built.

Think about a very strong safe. A burglar may not be able to crack the lock. But the burglar may listen to the clicks of the dial, or notice that it takes longer to reject some combinations than others, or shake the safe until something goes wrong. None of these attacks the steel.

Here are the types to know.

An implementation attack exploits a mistake in the software or hardware, such as weak random numbers, or a key left in memory. The algorithm may be perfectly good. It was just built badly.

A side-channel attack studies physical signs, such as power use, heat, sound or radio signals. Nobody is cooperating with the attacker. The device simply gives away information as it works.

A timing attack is a side-channel attack that measures how long operations take. Imagine a program that checks a password one letter at a time, and stops at the first wrong letter. An attacker can measure tiny differences in response time. A slightly slower response means more letters were correct. So the attacker can work out the password letter by letter.

Fault injection deliberately causes errors, for example with a power spike, heat or a laser, in order to make a device give up secrets or skip checks. Imagine pulling the plug at just the right moment, so that a door's lock skips its check.

The difference is important. Side-channel and timing attacks only observe. Fault injection actively disturbs.

Here are the defenses to know. Use tested libraries, and do not write your own. Make operations always take the same time, known as constant-time code. Use shielding, and tamper-resistant hardware that detects a voltage or temperature attack and erases its keys.

Here is a workplace example. A bank issues smart cards to its customers. A researcher measures the tiny variations in power that a card uses while signing, and recovers the key. This is called power analysis. The manufacturer responds by making the card's power use more uniform, and by adding random noise.

A manager should remember that a strong algorithm does not mean a strong product.

Here is what to take away. These attacks target the device or code, not the mathematics. Side channels observe, and fault injection disturbs.

studyNotes.heading: Man in the middle and pass the hash
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at two attacks on real-world communications and logins.

In a man-in-the-middle attack, or MITM, the attacker secretly sits between two parties. Each party thinks it is talking to the other. Think about passing notes through a third person. If that person is dishonest, they can read every note, and rewrite it before passing it on. You would never know.

Here is a workplace example. An employee connects to a fake wireless network in a coffee shop, set up by an attacker. All of the employee's traffic travels through the attacker's laptop. The attacker can read or change anything that is not properly protected.

The main defenses are digital certificates, which vouch for who owns a public key, and having both sides prove who they are. That is why staff must not click through browser certificate warnings. A warning may be the only sign that someone is in the middle. A related technique is replay, where the attacker captures a valid message and sends it again later. Timestamps and one-time values stop this.

Pass the hash is a credential attack on Windows networks. Windows can accept a stored password hash for authentication with the older NTLM method, which stands for NT LAN Manager. An attacker who steals the hash from memory can log in without ever knowing the password.

Think of a hotel that lets you collect your key if you show a photocopy of your booking form. The thief does not need your identity. A copy of the form is enough.

The hash is usually taken from the memory of a computer where a powerful account has recently logged in. The attacker then uses the hash to reach another computer, and repeats the process. This is called lateral movement.

The defenses are these.

- Least privilege, and separate admin accounts.
- Do not log in with admin accounts on ordinary computers.
- Use unique local admin passwords.
- Limit or turn off NTLM.

An attacker with the hash does not need to know what the password is.

A manager should see that the fix is mostly about administrative practice, and not about a new product.

Here is your takeaway. Man in the middle is defeated by certificates and mutual proof of identity, and pass the hash uses the hash itself, so limit where powerful accounts log in.

studyNotes.heading: Kerberos exploitation
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to look at attacks on Kerberos, which is the login system used by most Windows networks.

Kerberos is a network login system that uses tickets, like a wristband at a fair. You prove who you are once at the entrance, and you get a wristband. You then show that wristband at each ride, and you get a ticket for that ride.

A central server, the Key Distribution Center, or KDC, gives out the tickets. The wristband is called a ticket-granting ticket. It lets you ask for service tickets, which are the tickets for each individual service.

The tickets are protected by encryption, using keys derived from account passwords. That is what the attacks go after. Here are the four to know.

Kerberoasting: request a service ticket, take it offline and crack the service account's password. Any ordinary user can request such a ticket, which is why the attack is so popular. The defense is a long, random password on each service account.

Golden ticket: forge a ticket-granting ticket using the hash of the KRBTGT account, which is the account that signs those tickets. This gives wide control over the whole domain, the managed group of Windows computers and accounts. It is like stealing the machine that prints the wristbands.

Silver ticket: forge a service ticket with a service account's hash. This gives access to that one service. Because the forged ticket goes straight to the service, the central server may never see it, so it is harder to detect.

Pass the ticket: steal and reuse a valid ticket from a computer's memory.

The defenses are these. Keep tight control of domain controllers, the servers that handle logins. Monitor for unusual ticket activity. And after a compromise, reset the KRBTGT password twice, because the account remembers its previous password and tickets signed with either one remain valid until both have changed.

Here is a workplace example. An investigator finds that an attacker has copied the domain controller's database. The manager has to assume that the KRBTGT hash has been stolen. So the password must be reset twice, carefully and with a gap between the two resets, so that ordinary services are not broken.

Here is what to take away. Golden ticket uses the KRBTGT hash and controls the domain, while silver ticket uses a service hash and reaches one service.

studyNotes.heading: Ransomware
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we are going to look at ransomware, which is encryption being used against you.

Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts your files and demands payment. Think of a burglar who does not steal your furniture, but changes all the locks and then offers to sell you the key. Many gangs also steal the data first, and threaten to publish it. That is called double extortion. So even an organization with perfect backups can still be pressured.

It usually arrives through a phishing email, which is a message designed to trick someone, through stolen remote access accounts, or through a flaw that has not been patched.

Here is the best preparation.

- Offline or unchangeable backups, tested regularly.
- Patching, multi-factor login and staff awareness.
- Network segmentation, which divides the network into separate parts, to slow the spread.
- A rehearsed incident response plan.

Multi-factor login means proving who you are in more than one way, such as a password and a code from your phone.

Backups deserve special attention. Attackers now go looking for backups so that they can destroy them first. A widely taught approach is the 3-2-1 rule. Keep three copies of your data, on two different types of media, with one copy off site. A backup that has never been restored is only a hope, so test the restore.

During an attack, follow the plan. Isolate infected systems first. Do not simply switch everything off, because memory may hold useful evidence, and the plan should say how to handle this. Then tell the right people, including legal advisers, senior management, and regulators where the law requires.

Whether to pay is a decision for senior management, with legal advice. It is not a decision for the technical team. Paying does not guarantee recovery, and in some cases it may be illegal, for example if the group is under sanctions.

After recovery, find the root cause so that it does not happen again.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital is hit on a Sunday night. Staff follow a practised plan. Infected servers are cut off, clinics move to paper, and patient safety stays the first priority. Clean backups are restored over the following days, once the entry point has been closed.

Here is your takeaway. Prepare with tested offline backups, isolate first, leave payment to senior management, and fix the root cause.

keyTerms.meaning: Trying every possible key.
Attacker holds some original text and its encrypted form.
Attacker picks text to encrypt and studies the results.
Using how often letters appear to break a simple cipher.
Learning secrets from physical signs such as power or timing.
Forcing errors in a device to reveal secrets or skip checks.
Secretly sitting between two parties and relaying their messages.
Logging in with a stolen password hash instead of the password.
A forged Kerberos ticket made with the KRBTGT hash.
Malicious software that encrypts files and demands payment.

keyPoints: Attacks on mathematics are grouped by what the attacker holds.
Side-channel and fault attacks target the device, not the mathematics.
Pass the hash needs the hash, not the password.
Golden ticket uses the KRBTGT hash; silver ticket uses a service hash.
Offline, tested backups are the top ransomware defense.
topics.memoryHook: Golden ticket opens the whole fair. Silver ticket opens one ride.

question.prompt: A payment card maker finds that a researcher extracted a card's secret key by briefly dropping the card's power supply at exact moments, causing calculation errors. Which attack was used?
options: Fault injection
Frequency analysis
Chosen ciphertext
Brute force
question.explanation: Deliberately causing errors in a device is fault injection. A timing or side-channel attack is close, but those only observe the device. Here, the researcher actively disturbed it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An attacker has captured a large amount of encrypted traffic, but has no matching original text and cannot make the system encrypt anything. Which type of attack is the attacker limited to?
options: Ciphertext only
Known plaintext
Chosen plaintext
Chosen ciphertext
practiceQuestions.explanation: Having only the scrambled text is a ciphertext only attack, which is the hardest case for the attacker. Known plaintext is tempting, but that needs some original text as well.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A tester persuades a system to encrypt several messages of the tester's own choosing and then studies the results. Which attack is this?
options: Known plaintext
Frequency analysis
Chosen plaintext
Brute force
practiceQuestions.explanation: Choosing text to be encrypted and studying the results is a chosen plaintext attack. Known plaintext is tempting, but in that attack the attacker merely holds some original text and has no say in what it is.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An investigator studies an old coded letter and notices that one symbol appears far more often than the others. Which technique will MOST likely help the investigator decode it?
options: A birthday attack
A timing attack
A pass the hash attack
Frequency analysis
practiceQuestions.explanation: Counting how often symbols appear is frequency analysis, and it defeats simple substitution. A birthday attack is tempting because it also relies on statistics, but it is used to find hash collisions.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company still uses an older 128-bit hash for signing contracts. What is the MAIN concern with its short output?
options: It cannot be used on documents of more than one page
A birthday attack could find two documents with one hash
An attacker could read the original document from the hash
The hash reveals the private key of the signer
practiceQuestions.explanation: A short hash offers weak collision resistance, so two documents with the same hash could allow a forged signature. Reading the document from the hash is tempting, but hashes are one-way.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A program checks a stored code one character at a time and stops at the first wrong one. A tester uses small differences in response time to work out the code. What is the BEST fix?
options: Compare every character in a constant amount of time
Encrypt the network link between client and server
Add more characters to the code and rotate it monthly
Move the comparison to a more powerful server
practiceQuestions.explanation: Constant-time comparison removes the timing differences that leak information. A longer code is tempting, but it only slows the attacker slightly, because the leak would still reveal one character at a time.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security researcher uses a brief voltage drop to make a device skip its signature check during startup. How is this attack BEST classified?
options: A timing attack
A known plaintext attack
Fault injection
A meet-in-the-middle attack
practiceQuestions.explanation: Deliberately disturbing a device to cause errors is fault injection. A timing attack is tempting because it is also a physical attack, but it only observes the device and does not disturb it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An attacker takes a stored password hash from a workstation's memory and uses it to log in to a server, without ever learning the password. What should the security manager do to BEST reduce this risk?
options: Require users to choose much longer passwords
Install a stronger firewall at the network edge
Force every user to change passwords each week
Keep admin accounts off ordinary workstations and limit NTLM
practiceQuestions.explanation: Pass the hash uses the hash itself, so the defense is limiting where powerful accounts leave hashes and reducing NTLM. Longer passwords are tempting, but the attacker never needs to know the password.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Investigators conclude that attackers have obtained the hash of a domain's KRBTGT account. Which threat does this MOST directly enable?
options: A silver ticket for a single service
A golden ticket giving wide control of the domain
A chosen plaintext attack on the mail server
A rainbow table attack on staff passwords
practiceQuestions.explanation: The KRBTGT hash lets an attacker forge ticket-granting tickets, which is a golden ticket. A silver ticket is tempting because it also forges tickets, but it uses a service account's hash and reaches only one service.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During a security review, a team learns that any domain user can request tickets for a service account whose password is short. Which attack does this situation MOST invite?
options: Fault injection
Kerberoasting
Frequency analysis
Golden ticket
practiceQuestions.explanation: Kerberoasting requests a service ticket and cracks a weak service account password offline. Golden ticket is tempting because it is the best known Kerberos attack, but it needs the KRBTGT hash.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company is designing its defenses against ransomware. Which single measure gives the BEST chance of recovering data without paying?
options: A cyber insurance policy that covers ransom payments
Antivirus software on every staff workstation
Offline or unchangeable backups that are regularly tested
Annual awareness training on suspicious email
practiceQuestions.explanation: Tested offline backups cannot be encrypted by the attacker and can be relied upon. Antivirus software is tempting because it helps prevention, but the question is about recovery when prevention has failed.

topics.name: Site and facility design principles
topics.simpleExplanation: Physical security begins before the walls go up. Where you build matters, and so does how the building is laid out. Good design makes wrongdoing harder without needing a guard on every corner. Open views, clear paths and well-kept grounds tell people someone is watching. Inside, areas get more secure the deeper you go, like a castle with several rings of walls. Above all, the design must keep people safe, so they can always get out in an emergency.

studyNotes.heading: Plan the site first
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at how physical security starts before the first wall goes up.

Think about choosing a house. You look at the neighbourhood. You ask whether the river floods, how far the fire station is, and whether the road is safe at night. You would not buy first and ask later. Choosing a site for a building is exactly the same.

Begin with a risk assessment of the site. Good questions include these.

Is the area prone to floods, storms or earthquakes?

What is the local crime rate?

How close are the police, the fire service and the hospital?

Are there reliable power and network links, ideally from more than one provider?

Can visitors and vehicles be controlled?

Is a neighbour a danger, such as a chemical plant?

A few of these need explaining. If two network links enter the building through the same trench, one digger can cut both. So real redundancy means separate paths from separate providers. Redundancy simply means having a spare.

Do not forget about visibility, either. A site that is very easy to see from the road may invite unwanted attention. For a data centre, a plain and unmarked building is often the better choice, so that it does not advertise what is inside.

Involve security staff early. Changes are much cheaper at the drawing stage than after the building is finished. Security must also follow fire codes and building laws. Local law may decide things such as the number of exits, and a security design has to fit within that law.

Here is a workplace example. A company is choosing between two buildings for a new office and data room. The cheaper one sits on a flood plain and has one power supply. The more expensive one is on higher ground, near a fire station and has two separate power feeds. The security manager puts this comparison in plain business terms and presents it to the directors. The decision belongs to them, but the manager's job is to make sure they understand the risks.

As with all security work, the best time to deal with a problem is before it has been built in.

Here is what to take away. Assess the site before building or leasing it, check hazards, services and neighbours, and bring security into the plans from the very start.

studyNotes.heading: CPTED
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to look at a way of designing places so that crime becomes less attractive.

CPTED stands for Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design. It is usually said as sep-ted. It means shaping a place so that wrongdoing is harder and more likely to be noticed, without needing a guard on every corner. It has three main strategies.

- Natural access control: guide people with paths, fences, lighting and landscaping toward the correct entrance.
- Natural surveillance: make it easy to see and be seen. Use low bushes, open sightlines and windows facing the car park.
- Natural territorial reinforcement: show that the space is owned and cared for, with signs, tidy grounds and clear borders.

Think about a home with a garden. A clear front path leads visitors to your door, and that is access control. Low front hedges let neighbours see who is there, and that is surveillance. A tidy lawn and a name on the gate tell strangers that someone cares about this place, and that is territorial reinforcement.

The word natural is important. These strategies use the design of the place itself, and not extra guards or technology.

A well-kept site also signals that someone is paying attention. Broken lights and rubbish signal the opposite. So maintenance is often considered part of the approach.

Here is a workplace example. A school trims its hedges, puts one clear visitor path past the office window, and adds its name and signs along the fence. Fewer people wander in, and no extra guards were hired. Staff in the office can now see every visitor. The clearly marked boundary means a stranger is more likely to feel out of place.

Here is a second one. An office car park has a problem with break-ins, and it is hidden behind tall hedges and poorly lit. Before spending money on guards, the manager looks at the design. The hedges come down, lights go up, and the path to the entrance becomes the only obvious route.

As a manager, remember that this is often the cheapest and longest-lasting answer, because it deals with the cause and does not add a running cost.

Here is your takeaway. CPTED uses natural access control, natural surveillance and natural territorial reinforcement, so that the design of a place does much of the work of protecting it.

studyNotes.heading: Layers, zones and the order of defense
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at how to arrange security in layers. Think of a castle, with several rings of walls and the most valuable things at the centre.

Use zones, with more control the deeper you go. A typical layout is this.

- Public: car park and lobby.
- Reception or controlled: visitors signed in and escorted.
- Restricted: staff work areas needing a badge.
- High security: server rooms and evidence stores, with strict access and logging.

Each boundary should delay and detect. It is rarely possible to stop every attacker. But each layer can slow an attacker down, and give the defenders a chance to notice and respond.

A common way of teaching the order of physical defense runs like this.

- Deter: discourage the attempt.
- Deny: make entry difficult.
- Detect: notice the attempt.
- Delay: slow the attacker down.
- Respond: send people to deal with it.

Think about your home. A security sign deters. A locked door denies. An alarm detects. A strong inner door delays. And the police, or a neighbour, respond.

Here is a useful way of checking whether a design works. Add up how long the barriers will delay an intruder. Compare that with how long it will take someone to respond. If the police take ten minutes, and your barriers delay an intruder for three, then the design will not hold. You need more delay, or a faster response.

There is one more piece. An access control vestibule, also called a mantrap, is a small room with two doors. Only one door can open at a time. A person enters, the first door locks, identity is checked, and only then does the second door open. It stops tailgating, which is following an authorized person through a door. Piggybacking is a similar word, used when the authorized person knowingly lets someone through.

Here is a workplace example. A bank's head office has a public lobby. A receptionist signs visitors in and gives them a badge. Staff floors require an access card. The data room is behind a mantrap, and it requires both a card and a fingerprint. Each step in is more controlled than the last.

Here is what to take away. Controls should get stricter the deeper you go, and each layer should give you time to detect and respond.

studyNotes.heading: Perimeter protection
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to look at the outer edge of a site, where physical security first meets the outside world.

The perimeter is the outer boundary of the property. Its first job is to mark that boundary, and to make it clear that crossing it is a deliberate act.

Fences are often taught by height, in feet, since that is how the exam usually states them.

- Three to four feet: deters casual trespassers.
- Six to seven feet: too hard to climb easily.
- Eight feet or more, with barbed wire on top: deters determined intruders.

Think about a garden wall. A low wall tells a passing child that this is someone's garden. A very high wall tells a thief that getting in is going to be hard work.

A bollard is a short, solid post that stops vehicles. They let people walk through, but they prevent a vehicle from being driven into the building.

Lighting does two jobs. It deters, and it lets people see. It should be continuous, with no dark gaps. Lights must not point in a way that blinds the guards or the cameras.

Guards are flexible, and they can use judgment, which no machine can do. But they are costly, and they make mistakes. Dogs are a good deterrent, but they raise liability and safety concerns.

Cameras can deter, detect and record. Cameras that nobody watches, however, only help you after the event. CCTV, or closed-circuit television, is the usual term.

A perimeter intrusion detection system senses when someone touches or crosses the boundary, for example by detecting vibrations in a fence.

Gates should be few in number, and each one should be watched. Deliveries should be kept apart from staff and visitor entrances, so that a delivery lorry cannot simply follow a car inside.

Here is a workplace example. A warehouse has an eight foot fence, bollards in front of its main doors, continuous lighting and cameras on every side. A single vehicle gate is staffed by a guard who checks each driver against the day's delivery list. Each control supports the others.

As always, a manager needs to choose the mix based on risk, and not simply buy the most impressive equipment.

Here is your takeaway. Mark the boundary, slow people and vehicles down, light the area, and remember that human judgment is what guards add.

studyNotes.heading: Secure layout inside the building
studyNotes.body:
Now we are going to look at how the inside of a building should be laid out.

Think about where you would put your valuables at home. You would not leave them on a shelf by the front window. You would not store them under a leaking pipe. You would keep them in the middle of the house, somewhere dry and out of sight.

Good layout rules are these.

Put the server room near the centre of the building, away from outside walls.

Avoid basements, where floods reach, and top floors, where roofs leak.

Do not place it next to kitchens, toilets or water pipes.

Keep its walls running from the true floor to the true ceiling, so that nobody can climb over through the ceiling space or crawl under through a raised floor.

Give those walls a fire rating, which is usually at least one hour. That is how long they are expected to hold back a fire.

Limit entrances. Use few windows on sensitive areas.

Do not put up signs saying where the server room is.

Separate deliveries from staff entry.

Let us take one of these further. Many offices have a suspended ceiling, made of light tiles, with an empty space above it. If the wall of a secure room stops at the tiles, a person can lift a tile and climb across the top. That is why the wall must reach the true ceiling, which is the real structure of the building.

Doors matter too. A door to a secure room should be as strong as the wall around it. Think about which way a door should fail if power is lost. Fail-safe means it unlocks so that people can leave. Fail-secure means it stays locked to protect what is inside.

Safety comes first. Exits must be marked, and escape routes kept clear. Where a door's security and a person's life conflict, life wins. Emergency exits can be fitted with alarms, so that anyone using one is noticed.

Here is a workplace example. A company planning a new office wants the server room at the front, because the view is good for visitors. The security manager recommends a central room with no windows, away from plumbing.

Here is what to take away. Put sensitive rooms centrally, away from water and outside walls, build the walls full height, and never let security block escape.

studyNotes.heading: Bringing it together: a worked site review
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we are going to bring all of the ideas in this topic together by walking through a review of a real kind of site.

Imagine that a company has asked you to review a new branch office. You approach it as a manager, and you work from the outside in.

Step one is the site itself. You ask about flood history and local crime. You find that the building is on a slight hill, and that the nearest fire station is five minutes away. Good.

Step two is the perimeter. There is a car park at the side, screened by tall shrubs and poorly lit. That is a concern. You recommend trimming the shrubs and improving the lighting. That applies natural surveillance, from Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design.

Step three is the approach. Visitors are confused about where to go, and some walk to the side door. You recommend one clear path to the front entrance. That is natural access control.

Step four is the entrance. The lobby is public. Behind it, staff areas are opened with an access card. You find that one door is regularly propped open by smokers. You recommend an alarm on any door held open, and a place for them to go that does not defeat the control. You fix the cause, and not just the symptom.

Step five is the sensitive room. The server room sits against an outer wall, next to the staff kitchen. There is a wall that stops at the ceiling tiles. You recommend moving the room if possible. If that is not possible, then you recommend extending the walls to the true ceiling, and adding leak detection. Those are compensating controls.

Step six is life safety. An exit in the stockroom is blocked by boxes. You raise this first, because people's safety comes before everything else. The boxes are moved that same day.

Step seven is reporting. You give the directors a short list, ordered by risk, with costs and recommendations. You remind them that the decision to accept any remaining risk is theirs.

Notice what this review did. It did not begin with buying equipment. It looked at the design, it worked inward, and it fixed safety first.

Here is your takeaway. Review a site from the outside in, use design before adding cost, fix what endangers people first, and leave risk acceptance with management.

keyTerms.meaning: Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design: using layout to discourage crime.
Guiding people to the right entrances through design.
Designing so that people can easily see and be seen.
Showing that a space is owned and cared for.
Areas with increasing levels of control.
A two-door room where only one door opens at a time; also called an access control vestibule.
Following an authorized person through a door without permission.

keyPoints: Assess the site before building or leasing it.
CPTED uses access control, surveillance and territorial reinforcement.
Controls should get stricter the deeper you go.
Place server rooms centrally, away from water and outside walls.
Life safety always beats security.
topics.memoryHook: CPTED is ASK: Access guided, Seen by others, Kept and owned.

question.prompt: A small company has had thefts from cars in a poorly lit side car park hidden behind tall hedges. Management wants a low-cost lasting improvement based on environmental design. What should the security manager recommend FIRST?
options: Hire a guard to patrol the car park at night
Buy insurance to cover staff vehicles in the car park
Trim the hedges and improve the lighting for clear views
Install a biometric lock on the building's main entrance
question.explanation: Trimming hedges and adding light is natural surveillance, a core CPTED strategy, and it fixes the cause of the problem cheaply. A guard is tempting, but it is an ongoing cost and does not change the design that hides the crime.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company is choosing a site for a new data centre. Which activity should be carried out FIRST?
options: Selecting the access control vendor
Assessing risks at the proposed locations
Designing the layout of the server room
Calculating the size of backup generators
practiceQuestions.explanation: A site risk assessment comes before any detailed design or purchasing. Designing the server room is tempting because it is important, but there is no point designing for a site that should not be used.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A hospital trims its shrubs and places windows so that staff can easily see the car park. Which CPTED strategy does this BEST represent?
options: Natural access control
Natural territorial reinforcement
Natural surveillance
Target hardening
practiceQuestions.explanation: Making it easy to see and be seen is natural surveillance. Natural access control is tempting because it also concerns the car park, but it is about guiding where people go.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A college adds its name along a boundary, keeps the grounds tidy, and marks clearly where campus property begins. Which CPTED strategy is being applied?
options: Natural territorial reinforcement
Natural surveillance
Natural access control
Defense in depth
practiceQuestions.explanation: Showing that a space is owned and cared for is territorial reinforcement. Natural surveillance is tempting because tidy grounds can be easier to see, but the aim here is to show ownership.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Staff are observed holding secure doors open for colleagues who forgot their badges. Which control would MOST directly prevent people from following others through?
options: A printed reminder placed next to the doors
A camera recording the doorway
A higher perimeter fence around the site
An access control vestibule
practiceQuestions.explanation: A vestibule lets one person through at a time and physically stops tailgating. A camera is tempting because it records the event, but it only detects after the fact and does not prevent anyone from following.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security manager calculates that barriers at a warehouse would delay an intruder for three minutes, but that the response team takes ten minutes to arrive. What is the BEST conclusion?
options: The design is sound, as barriers are in place
Delay must be increased, or response made faster
The response team should be disbanded as too slow
Barriers can be removed, as they are not effective
practiceQuestions.explanation: Barriers should hold an intruder until the response arrives. The first option is tempting because the barriers exist, but three minutes of delay does not match a ten minute response.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A site needs a fence that will discourage determined intruders. Which option BEST fits that need?
options: A three foot fence
A four foot fence
A six foot fence
An eight foot fence with barbed wire
practiceQuestions.explanation: Eight feet or more with barbed wire is the level taught for determined intruders. A six foot fence is tempting because it is hard to climb, but it is not the level described for a determined attacker.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A building manager wants to stop a vehicle from being driven through the glass front of an office, while allowing people to walk freely. Which control is BEST?
options: Bollards
Turnstiles
A mantrap
Motion sensors
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bollards stop vehicles while allowing people through. A mantrap is tempting because it is a strong entry control, but it controls individual people at a door and does nothing to stop a vehicle.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company is deciding where to place a new server room in a multi-storey office. Which location is BEST?
options: The basement, because it is out of public view
The top floor, because it is hard to reach
A central room on a middle floor, away from plumbing
A room by the main entrance, for easy deliveries
practiceQuestions.explanation: A central room on a middle floor avoids floods, roof leaks and outside walls. The basement is tempting because it is hidden, but basements are at risk from flooding.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A secure room's walls stop at the suspended ceiling tiles. An auditor flags this as a weakness. What is the MOST appropriate correction?
options: Add a brighter light above the secure room door
Extend the walls up to the true ceiling
Install a sign restricting entry to authorized staff
Change the ceiling tiles to a darker colour
practiceQuestions.explanation: Full-height walls stop someone climbing over through the ceiling space. A sign is tempting because it is cheap, but it is a deterrent and does not close the physical gap.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A site review finds a blocked fire exit, a weak lock on a store cupboard and old security cameras. What should the security manager address FIRST?
options: The old cameras, since they provide evidence
The weak lock, as theft might occur
All three items, ordered by purchase cost
The blocked fire exit, since lives are at risk
practiceQuestions.explanation: People's safety comes first, so the blocked exit must be fixed before anything else. The cameras are tempting because they support investigations, but no security benefit outweighs a risk to life.

topics.name: Site and facility controls
topics.simpleExplanation: Important rooms need their own protection. A wiring closet needs a lock. A server room needs clean power, steady air and the right fire system. Tapes and drives need safe storage, and evidence needs a record of every person who touched it. You should also know the names of electrical problems and the classes of fire. The most important rule never changes. Protecting people comes before protecting equipment, even if that means losing the data centre.

studyNotes.heading: Wiring closets and server rooms
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to look at how to protect the rooms that hold networking and computing equipment.

A wiring closet is a small room that holds the cables and switches for one floor. It is also called an intermediate distribution facility, because it distributes network connections between the main equipment room and the desks on that floor.

Think about the fuse box in a house. It is small and easy to forget. But anyone who gets to it can turn off everything. A wiring closet is the same. A person with access can plug in a small listening device, or simply pull out cables. Attackers know that it is often the least protected room in the building.

Lock wiring closets, and log who goes in. Do not use them for storage, as they often end up being used for mops and cardboard boxes, which is both a fire risk and a reason for cleaners to go in and out. Keep any network ports that are not in use switched off. Cable trays and cables running through shared spaces should also be protected.

Server rooms and data centres hold the systems themselves. They need strict access, cameras, logs and escorted visitors. Keep the number of people with access small, and review that list regularly. Nobody should be there just because it is convenient. Everyone who enters should have a reason, and any visitor should be with an escort at all times.

Data centres often use extra layers. These include access cards together with a second check such as a fingerprint, locked cabinets inside the room, and cameras inside the aisles. A cabinet lock matters when several teams or customers share a room.

If you use someone else's data centre, known as co-location, you should still ask to see how their access controls work, and you should read the audit reports.

Here is a workplace example. A company's audit finds a wiring closet with an unlocked door, boxes on the floor, and an unknown device plugged into a switch. The security manager has the room cleared and locked, starts a key log, investigates the device as a possible incident, and adds wiring closets to the quarterly inspection list.

Here is what to take away. Wiring closets are small but powerful, so lock them and log them. Server rooms need strict access, cameras, logs and escorted visitors.

studyNotes.heading: Media storage, evidence and work areas
studyNotes.body:
