Now we will look at three more kinds of space: where media is stored, where evidence is stored, and where people work.

Media storage holds tapes and drives. Think of a library of family photographs. If you do not label them, you cannot find them. If you leave them in a hot attic, they spoil. If anyone can walk off with them, they will go missing.

So label media, control check-out, and protect it from heat and magnetic fields. Keep backup media at a different site from the system it protects, so that a single fire cannot destroy both. When media is no longer needed, sanitize it, which means removing the data completely, before reuse. If it holds very sensitive data, destroy it, and keep a record of that.

Evidence storage must keep a chain of custody, which is a record of who handled an item, when and why. Think of a relay race, where the baton must be accounted for at every hand-over. If there is a gap in the record, a court may refuse to accept the evidence.

Use a dedicated locked room with very few keyholders. Log each entry. Protect the items from damage, and keep digital evidence away from anything that could alter it.

Here is a workplace example. After a suspected fraud, an investigator takes a laptop from an employee's desk. It is placed in a sealed evidence bag, labelled and signed. It is logged into a locked evidence room. When a forensic examiner collects it a week later, both people sign the log. Every movement has been recorded.

Restricted and work areas are where staff handle information every day. They should use badges, clean desk rules and visitor escorts. Higher sensitivity needs tighter control. A clean desk rule means papers are locked away at the end of the day. Screens should lock when staff walk away, and should be placed so that passers-by cannot read them.

Some areas need even stronger protection. A sensitive compartmented information facility, or SCIF, is a specially built room for handling highly classified information. It is shielded and strictly controlled, and phones are usually left outside.

Here is your takeaway. Label and control your media, keep an unbroken chain of custody for evidence, and match work area controls to how sensitive the information is.

studyNotes.heading: Power problems and how to handle them
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to learn the names of electrical problems, and the protections against them. The exam expects the exact pairs.

Think about the water coming from a tap. It might stop altogether. It might slow to a trickle. Or it might come out so strongly that it damages your pipes. Electricity can do all of the same things.

Here are the pairs. In each pair, the first name is short, and the second is long.

- Fault: short loss of power. Blackout: long loss of power.
- Sag: short low voltage. Brownout: long low voltage.
- Spike: short high voltage. Surge: long high voltage.

There are two more terms.

- Inrush: a sudden rise when equipment first switches on.
- Noise: unwanted interference on the line.

Noise includes electromagnetic interference, often caused by nearby motors, and radio frequency interference. Cable shielding and keeping data cables away from power cables both help.

Here are the protections.

A UPS, or Uninterruptible Power Supply, provides batteries for a short time. It is usually enough to shut down cleanly, or to start a generator.

A generator provides longer-term power. It needs fuel and regular tests. A generator that has not been tested may not start when it is needed. Check how long your fuel will last, and arrange for more to be delivered in an emergency.

Surge protectors and power conditioners guard against spikes and clean up the supply.

Two power feeds, ideally from separate sources, protect against failure of one supply. Redundant power supplies in each server mean that one failure does not stop the server.

Here is the worked sequence of a power cut. The main supply fails. In that first moment, the Uninterruptible Power Supply takes over without a break. A few seconds later, the generator starts. Once the generator is running steadily, it takes over the load, and the batteries recharge. When mains power returns, the system switches back. A battery alone lasts only a short time, so without a generator, the servers would have to shut down.

Here is a workplace example. A company tests its generator once a year, without load. During a real outage, the generator starts but cannot carry the full load, and systems go down. The fix is regular testing under a realistic load.

Here is what to take away. Short problems are fault, sag and spike. Long problems are blackout, brownout and surge.

studyNotes.heading: HVAC, water and other environmental issues
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at keeping the air, the temperature and the water under control.

HVAC means Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning. Servers need steady conditions. Think of a pet fish. It is not only the water that matters. The water has to be at the right temperature, and it has to stay that way.

Here are the figures to know.

- Temperature: about 18 to 27 degrees Celsius, which is 64 to 81 degrees Fahrenheit.
- Humidity: commonly taught as 40 to 60 percent.

Why does humidity matter? Too low causes static electricity. A small spark from a person's finger can damage a circuit. Too high causes condensation and corrosion, as water settles on the equipment.

Use positive air pressure, so that dust and smoke are pushed out when doors open. Positive pressure means that the air pressure inside the room is a little higher than outside. Air flows outward when a door is opened. Think about a soap bubble being blown from the inside, always pushing outward.

Give the server room its own controls for this equipment, so that a problem in the main building does not affect it. It should also be possible to shut it down quickly in a fire, because air movement feeds a fire and spreads smoke.

For environmental risks, use water leak sensors, raised equipment, bracing against earthquakes and shutoff valves. Know where the water enters the building. Everyone who may need to shut off the water should know exactly where the valves are. A burst pipe at night needs a quick response.

Think about wind and storms too. Storms can damage roofs, bring down power lines and block roads, so that staff cannot reach the site. Plans should allow for this.

Here is a workplace example. A server room has been running at 45 percent humidity. An air conditioning unit fails during a heatwave. Sensors send an alert to the on-call engineer, who arranges a temporary cooling unit, and shuts down non-essential servers. Because the room has monitoring, the problem is found early, before the equipment is damaged.

A manager should make sure that the utilities are monitored, and that somebody is responsible for acting on the alerts.

Here is your takeaway. Keep temperature and humidity steady, use positive pressure, and know where the water comes in.

studyNotes.heading: Fire: prevention, detection and classes
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to look at how fires start, how we detect them, and the classes of fire.

Fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen, and a chemical reaction keeps it going. Remove one and it stops. Think about a candle. Blow it out and you remove the heat. Put a glass over it and you remove the oxygen.

Prevention comes first. Good housekeeping removes things that can burn. Staff are trained. Fire-resistant materials are used. Fire doors are kept shut, and they are never propped open.

A fire usually grows in four stages.

- Incipient: the air begins to change, with no visible smoke.
- Smoke: smoke becomes visible.
- Flame: flames can be seen.
- Heat: high heat builds up, and damage spreads.

Detectors are matched to these stages. Ionization and photoelectric smoke detectors notice smoke early. Heat detectors work when a set temperature is reached, or when the temperature rises very quickly. Flame detectors sense the light given off by a flame. Fire detection should alert people early.

United States fire classes are as follows.

- Class A: ordinary items such as paper and wood. Use water or foam.
- Class B: flammable liquids such as petrol. Use carbon dioxide, foam or dry powder.
- Class C: live electrical equipment. Use carbon dioxide or clean gas, never water.
- Class D: burning metals. Use dry powder made for metals.
- Class K: kitchen oils. Use a wet chemical.

A simple memory aid goes like this. Class A leaves ash. Class B comes in barrels. Class C is current. Class D is dust of metal. Class K is the kitchen. Other parts of the world use different letters, so take care if you see a non-United States classification.

Why never water on Class C? Because water conducts electricity, and it can injure the person who is holding the hose. If the power is cut off first, then the fire is no longer an electrical one, and it can be treated as an ordinary fire.

Here is a workplace example. A small fire starts in a power supply inside a server room. A smoke detector raises the alarm. A trained member of staff uses a carbon dioxide extinguisher, because it will not damage equipment or conduct electricity.

Here is what to take away. Fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen, and the classes are A, B, C, D and K.

studyNotes.heading: Fire suppression and protecting people
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we are going to look at the systems that put fires out, and at the priority that sits above everything else.

There are four water sprinkler systems to know.

- Wet pipe: always full of water. It is the simplest, but leaks are a risk.
- Dry pipe: holds air until needed. Good for freezing areas.
- Preaction: fills with water only after a detector triggers, and then releases when a sprinkler head melts. It is the best water choice for data centres.
- Deluge: all heads open at once for a large release of water. Used for high-hazard areas.

Let us look closely at preaction, because two separate events have to happen. First, a detector senses a fire, which lets water into the pipes. Second, a sprinkler head melts from the heat, and the water comes out. If a pipe is damaged, or if a detector gives a false alarm, then nothing is released onto the servers.

Gas systems protect electronics, and they leave the equipment usable.

Clean agents such as FM-200 and Inergen leave no residue. FM-200 absorbs heat. Inergen is a mix of inert gases that lowers oxygen to a level that will not support fire, while remaining breathable for people for a short time.

Halon is no longer produced under the Montreal Protocol, because it harms the ozone layer.

Carbon dioxide removes oxygen and can kill people, so use it only in unoccupied areas or with a warning delay. A warning delay gives people time to get out before the gas is released.

Cut electrical power before releasing water. An emergency power off switch, near the door of the room, lets staff do that quickly.

The exam will always come back to this point. Protecting people comes before protecting equipment, even if that means losing the data centre. If an exam option says stay behind to save the server, it is wrong. People leave first.

Train staff, run drills and make sure everyone can get out. Fire wardens should be named for each area, and everyone should know the meeting point.

Here is a workplace example. A company choosing a system for its new server room selects a clean agent, with preaction sprinklers behind it to meet the fire code.

Here is your takeaway. Preaction is the best water choice for data centres, carbon dioxide can kill, and people always come first.

keyTerms.meaning: A record of who handled evidence, when and why.
Short and long periods of low voltage.
Short and long periods of high voltage.
Short and long losses of power.
Uninterruptible Power Supply: batteries that give short-term power.
Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning.
Air flows outward when a door opens, keeping out dust and smoke.
A two-step water sprinkler system, best for data centres.
A fire-suppressing gas that leaves no residue, such as FM-200.

keyPoints: People's safety always comes first.
Short problems are fault, sag and spike; long ones are blackout, brownout and surge.
Fire classes are A, B, C, D and K.
Preaction is the best water option for data centres.
CO2 is dangerous to people, so it needs a warning delay.
topics.memoryHook: Fire classes: Ash, Barrel, Current, Dust of metal, Kitchen. Power: short names first (fault, sag, spike), and the long ones have longer names (blackout, brownout, surge).

question.prompt: A data centre wants a water-based fire system but worries that a damaged pipe or a single false alarm will soak its servers. Which system BEST addresses this concern?
options: Wet pipe, because water is immediately ready in the pipes
Preaction, because two events must occur before water flows
Deluge, because every sprinkler head opens at the same time
Dry pipe, because the pipes are safer in freezing locations
question.explanation: Preaction needs a detector to trigger and then a sprinkler head to open, so one mistake does not release water. Dry pipe is tempting because the pipes hold air, but it is designed for cold areas and lacks the detector step.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An audit finds a wiring closet left unlocked and being used to store cleaning supplies. What should the security manager require FIRST?
options: Replace all of the network switches with newer models
Lock the closet, restrict access and remove the supplies
Install a smoke detector and record the finding
Hire a guard to watch the corridor during office hours
practiceQuestions.explanation: Locking the room, restricting access and clearing it addresses the actual weakness. A guard is tempting because it adds visible protection, but it is a costly way of doing what a lock and an access list do better.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A hard drive taken as evidence in a fraud case passes between three staff members, but one transfer is not recorded. What is the MOST significant consequence?
options: The drive will need to be encrypted again
The drive must be sanitized before further use
The evidence may not be accepted in court
The evidence must be moved to a colder room
practiceQuestions.explanation: A gap in the chain of custody can make evidence unreliable and inadmissible. Sanitizing is tempting because it is a familiar media control, but sanitizing would destroy the evidence altogether.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company stores its backup tapes in the same room as the servers those tapes protect. What is the MAIN concern?
options: One fire could destroy both servers and backups
The tapes will slow down the servers in that room
Staff will be confused about which tape to use
The room's humidity will be raised by the tapes
practiceQuestions.explanation: Backups kept with the system they protect can be lost in the same event, so they should be stored elsewhere. Staff confusion is tempting because labelling matters, but the main risk is losing everything at once.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A voltage monitor records a period of several hours when the supply stayed lower than normal. What is this problem called?
options: Sag
Fault
Surge
Brownout
practiceQuestions.explanation: Prolonged low voltage is a brownout. A sag is tempting because it is also low voltage, but a sag is short.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A server experiences a momentary and very brief loss of electrical power, and supply then returns. Which term BEST describes this?
options: Fault
Blackout
Spike
Inrush
practiceQuestions.explanation: A short loss of power is a fault. Blackout is tempting because power was lost, but a blackout is a long loss.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A data centre's humidity has been falling steadily, and engineers are worried. Which problem is MOST likely if it continues?
options: Condensation on circuit boards
Corrosion of connector pins
Water pooling beneath the floor
Static electricity damaging equipment
practiceQuestions.explanation: Low humidity causes static electricity. Condensation is tempting because humidity is involved, but condensation and corrosion come from humidity that is too high.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A fire has started in live electrical equipment in a server room. Which extinguishing agent is MOST appropriate?
options: A water hose
A wet chemical
Carbon dioxide
Water-based foam
practiceQuestions.explanation: Class C fires need a non-conductive agent such as carbon dioxide or clean gas. Water-based foam is tempting because foam works on some fires, but it conducts electricity and could injure the person using it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A restaurant kitchen's cooking oil catches fire. Which fire class is this, and which agent is BEST?
options: Class A, using water
Class K, using a wet chemical
Class C, using clean gas
Class B, using dry powder
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cooking oils are Class K, and a wet chemical is the right agent. Class B is tempting because oil is a liquid, but cooking oils are treated as their own class.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A site in a very cold climate needs a sprinkler system for an unheated storage building where the pipes must not freeze. Which system is BEST?
options: Wet pipe
Deluge
Halon
Dry pipe
practiceQuestions.explanation: A dry pipe system holds air until needed, so the pipes do not freeze. Deluge is tempting because it is a water system, but it is intended for high-hazard areas and does not address freezing.

practiceQuestions.prompt: During a fire in an unoccupied data hall, an engineer proposes re-entering the room to remove backup drives before the carbon dioxide system discharges. What should the manager instruct?
options: Allow it, if the engineer works as quickly as possible
Allow it, if a second engineer waits at the door
Do not allow it, as nobody should enter the room
Do not allow it, until the drives have been logged
practiceQuestions.explanation: Carbon dioxide can kill, and people's safety comes before any data. The second option is tempting because it sounds cautious, but no precaution justifies sending a person into a room that is about to discharge gas.

topics.name: Information system lifecycle
topics.simpleExplanation: A system has a life, much like a house. Someone wants it, plans it, builds it, connects it, inspects it, moves in, maintains it, and one day pulls it down. Security must be part of every stage. Fixing a problem in the plan is cheap. Fixing it after people have moved in is expensive. The exam expects you to know the order of the stages and what security should do during each one, including safely ending the system's life.

studyNotes.heading: The stages in order
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we are going to see the whole life of an information system, and learn its stages in order.

A system lifecycle is the full set of stages in a system's life. Think about building a house and living in it. Somebody wants a home. An architect plans it. Builders construct it. An inspector checks it. The family moves in and looks after it for years. One day, it is pulled down. A system follows the same path.

Here is the order to learn.

- 1. Stakeholder needs and requirements definition
- 2. Requirements analysis
- 3. Architectural design
- 4. Development or implementation
- 5. Integration
- 6. Verification and validation
- 7. Transition or deployment
- 8. Operations and maintenance, also called sustainment
- 9. Retirement or disposal

Stakeholders are the people with an interest in the system, such as users, owners, regulators and customers.

Now here is the main idea that the exam is testing. Security belongs in every stage, starting at the first. It should not be added at the end.

Think about the cost of a change. Moving a window on a drawing costs almost nothing. Moving a window after the house has been built costs a great deal. Fixing a security flaw at the design stage is cheap. Fixing it after thousands of customers are using the system is expensive, and it may be too late to avoid harm.

Here is what security does in each stage, in short.

In the needs stage, security identifies the data, the laws and the level of risk that is acceptable.

In analysis, it turns those needs into testable requirements.

In design, it models threats and chooses controls.

In development, it applies secure coding.

In integration, it tests how the parts work together.

In verification and validation, it proves that the controls work.

In transition, it hardens the system and gets formal approval.

In operations, it patches, monitors and manages change.

In retirement, it protects and removes the data.

Here is a workplace example. A company rushes a new customer portal to market, and it asks security to look at it one week before launch. Testing finds a basic design flaw. The launch is delayed by months. Had security been involved from the start, the flaw would have been caught on paper.

Here is what to take away. Learn the nine stages in order, and remember that security belongs in every one of them.

studyNotes.heading: Needs and requirements analysis
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look closely at the first two stages, where the most important decisions are made.

In the stage of stakeholder needs, you ask what the business wants. Find the data involved, the laws that apply and how much risk the owner accepts. Get management support now, because security needs funds and authority.

Think about asking an architect to build you a house. The architect's first questions are about your family. How many people will live there? Do you need a ramp for a wheelchair? How much can you spend? It would be a mistake to start drawing before asking those things.

For security, the questions include these. What data will this system hold? How sensitive is it? Which laws apply? Who are the users? What is the harm if the system stops, or if the data is stolen or changed? Who owns this system, and who will accept its risk?

Do not forget to include all of the stakeholders. Users know how the work is really done. Lawyers know the regulations. Operations staff know what is hard to support.

In requirements analysis, you turn those needs into clear statements that can be tested. Let us look at the difference. The word secure cannot be tested. The sentence, lock the account after five failed logins, can be tested.

Here is a useful habit. For each statement, ask yourself how you would prove that it has been met. If you cannot answer that, then the statement needs rewriting.

Here is a worked example. A clinic wants a new patient booking system.

The need is this. Patient information must be private, and staff must be able to book appointments quickly.

The requirements become these. All patient records are encrypted when stored. Each staff member has an individual login. Each view of a record is logged. A booking screen appears within two seconds.

Notice that last requirement. It has nothing to do with security on its face, but it matters. If the secure method is too slow, then staff will look for ways around it.

Requirements also have to be traceable. That means each requirement is linked to the need it came from and to the test that proves it.

Here is your takeaway. Start with what stakeholders need and how much risk they accept, and then write requirements that can be tested and traced.

studyNotes.heading: Architectural design and development
studyNotes.body:
Next we are going to look at how the plan is drawn up, and how the system is built.

Architectural design means planning the structure of a system. Think about the drawings for a house. They decide where the walls go, where the electricity runs, and how many doors there are. Changing those things later is very difficult.

Do threat modeling here, which means thinking through what could go wrong. Apply secure design principles such as least privilege, which means only the access needed, and defense in depth, which means several layers of protection. Decide which controls go where.

Design is where the big decisions are made. Should the system store card numbers at all, or should a specialist payment company hold them instead? Where will the keys be kept? Which parts face the internet? Which parts must be kept apart? A system that never stores card numbers cannot have them stolen.

A design should also be reviewed by someone who did not create it.

The second stage here is development, also called implementation. It means building the system, using secure coding standards, code reviews and approved libraries. A library is a set of ready-made and tested code that a developer can reuse.

Here are some common practices.

Follow a coding standard, so that developers avoid known mistakes.

Have a second developer review the code. This is a human check.

Use tools to examine the code automatically. Static testing reads the code without running it. Dynamic testing runs the program and tries to break it.

Keep the code in a controlled store, so that every change is recorded and can be traced to a person.

Keep development, testing and live systems apart. And do not use real customer data for testing, unless it has been properly masked. Masking replaces sensitive values with harmless ones.

Keep track of third-party components too, because a flaw in a library becomes a flaw in your product. A software bill of materials is a list of what your product contains.

Here is a workplace example. A team building a hospital application finds at design stage that one service will need to reach every other service. They redesign it, so that each service has only the access it needs.

Here is what to take away. Make the big security decisions at design, and build with standards, reviews and tested components.

studyNotes.heading: Integration, verification and validation
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we are going to look at how the parts are joined together, and at how we prove that the system is right.

Integration means joining the parts together, and testing the connections. Parts that are safe alone may be unsafe once joined, for example if one trusts another without checking.

Think about the plumber and the electrician working on a house. Each one's work may be fine alone. But if the pipe goes through the same space as the cable, you have a new problem that neither of them created alone.

In the workplace, a web application may check the user's identity carefully, and pass the request to a billing service. If the billing service simply accepts anything from anyone on the network, then an attacker who reaches it directly can skip the identity check.

Verification and validation are different, and the exam likes this difference.

- Verification asks: did we build the system right? It checks the system against the written requirements.
- Validation asks: did we build the right system? It checks that the system meets the real needs of the users.

A memory aid is that verification looks at the document, and validation looks at the people.

Here is an everyday example. You order a cake for a birthday, and you write down chocolate, with one candle. The baker makes exactly that. That passes verification. But your child is allergic to chocolate, and it is the wrong cake for the party. It fails validation. The baker did what the paper said. The paper was wrong.

So a system can pass verification and still fail validation. It may match a flawed specification perfectly.

Here is a workplace example. A company's specification says that the expense system must require a manager's approval for each claim. Testers confirm that it does. That is verification. In practice, the company's managers are often away travelling, and claims are stuck for weeks. The system does not meet the real need. That is a validation failure.

For security, verification might include checking that every requirement has a passing test. Validation might include a penetration test, which is an authorized simulated attack, and trials with real users to see whether the controls work in practice.

Here is your takeaway. Parts that are safe alone may be unsafe when joined, verification means built right, and validation means the right thing was built.

studyNotes.heading: Transition, operations and maintenance
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at the moment a system goes live, and at the long period that follows.

Transition, also called deployment, means moving the system into live use. Think about moving into a new home. You change the locks, you check the smoke alarms, you learn how the heating works, and you make sure that you can leave quickly in an emergency.

Harden the system, meaning turn off everything not needed. Plan a way back if something fails. This is called a rollback plan. Train the users, and get formal approval. A senior manager accepts the remaining risk. Earlier in this domain we called that authorization, and it comes after the technical assessment.

Operations and maintenance is the next stage, and it is also called sustainment. It is usually the longest stage. A house is built in a few months, and lived in for decades. A system may be in service for many years.

The work of this stage includes the following.

Patch, which means install updates, after testing them.

Monitor, using logs and alerts.

Back up, and test recovery.

Review who has access, and remove what is no longer needed.

Reassess risk regularly, because threats change.

Two processes deserve particular attention. Change management means each change is reviewed, approved, tested and recorded. Configuration management means keeping systems at a known setup, so that you can notice if something has drifted.

Here is why this matters. Think about someone in a family quietly moving the fuse box without telling anyone. Everything seems fine, until the day there is a problem and nobody can find it. Unrecorded changes cause outages, and they also hide attackers.

Here is the order for a normal change. Someone makes a request. It is reviewed for risk. It is approved. It is tested. It is scheduled and carried out. The records are updated. In an emergency, the steps can be shortened, but the review still happens afterwards.

Here is a workplace example. An administrator changes a firewall rule on a Friday night to fix a problem, without any record. Weeks later, an attacker uses that opening. No one can say who made the change, or why. A proper change process would have shown the risk.

Here is what to take away. A senior manager approves the go-live, operations is usually the longest stage, and every change is reviewed, approved, tested and recorded.

studyNotes.heading: Retirement, and a worked example from start to finish
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at how a system's life ends, and then follow one system through every stage.

Retirement, or disposal, means ending the system safely. Think about moving out of a house. You take your valuables, you shred your old letters, you hand back the keys, and you tell the post office.

Here are the steps.

- Check how long the law requires data to be kept.
- Move or archive the data that must stay.
- Sanitize or destroy storage. Keep a record.
- Remove accounts, certificates and firewall rules.
- Tell the stakeholders and update the inventory.

Sanitizing has levels. Clearing overwrites data, to protect against ordinary recovery tools. Purging uses stronger methods, to protect against laboratory recovery. Destroying physically ruins the media. A degausser, which uses a powerful magnetic field, works on magnetic drives, but it does not work on solid state drives. Cryptographic erasure, which means destroying the encryption keys, is another option.

Forgotten accounts and firewall rules are common leftovers. An old connection that nobody remembers is a door left open.

Now we will follow one system through the stages. A shop wants to sell online.

- Needs: the owner wants online orders and must follow card payment rules.
- Analysis: card data must be encrypted, and staff need individual logins.
- Design: a payment company will handle card numbers, so the shop never stores them.
- Development: developers use a tested library and review each other's code.
- Integration: the store is joined to the payment service and tested.
- Verification: testers confirm each written requirement is met.
- Validation: real staff and customers confirm it works for them.
- Deployment: the owner approves the risk, and the store goes live.
- Operations: patches, monitoring and backups continue.
- Retirement: data is kept as the law requires, then disks are wiped and accounts removed.

Notice how a single good decision at the design stage made the later stages easier. Because the shop never held card numbers, it had fewer rules to follow in operations, and it had fewer worries at retirement.

As a manager, plan for the end at the start. Ask the vendor how you will get your data back, and how it will be destroyed.

Here is your takeaway. Retirement means checking retention, moving the data that must stay, sanitizing or destroying storage, and removing all access. Security runs through every stage, from the first idea to the last wiped disk.

keyTerms.meaning: Anyone with an interest in the system.
Turning needs into clear, testable statements.
Joining the parts and testing how they work together.
Did we build it right? Checks against the written requirements.
Did we build the right thing? Checks against real user needs.
Moving a system into live use.
Reviewing, approving, testing and recording every change.
Remove data from storage so that it cannot be recovered.

keyPoints: Security belongs in every stage, starting at the first.
Verification means built right; validation means the right thing was built.
Operations is usually the longest stage.
Retirement includes retention checks, sanitizing and removing access.
topics.memoryHook: Needs, Analysis, Design, Develop, Integrate, Verify, Transition, Operate, Retire: think of the house from the first idea to the wrecking ball.

question.prompt: Testers confirm that a new clinic booking system meets every item in its written specification. When nurses begin using it, they find it cannot handle urgent same-day appointments, which they need daily. Which activity did NOT succeed?
options: Integration
Verification
Retirement
Validation
question.explanation: The system matches the specification, so verification passed. It does not meet the users' real need, so validation failed. Verification is tempting because testing took place, but that testing only compared the system with the document.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A project team is identifying the data a new system will hold, the laws that apply and how much risk the owner will accept. Which lifecycle stage is this?
options: Architectural design
Stakeholder needs and requirements definition
Verification and validation
Transition
practiceQuestions.explanation: Understanding data, law and risk appetite happens at the first stage. Architectural design is tempting because it is also early, but design depends on knowing these needs first.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A project's security requirement says only that the system must be secure. What is the BEST action for the security manager?
options: Approve it, as it covers every possible threat
Add the word strongly to make the requirement firmer
Rewrite it as specific statements that can be tested
Remove it, since security belongs in the design stage
practiceQuestions.explanation: Requirements must be clear and testable. Approving it is tempting because it sounds complete, but nobody could ever prove that it had been met.

practiceQuestions.prompt: At which stage is it generally LEAST expensive to correct a security weakness?
options: Operations and maintenance
Transition or deployment
Requirements and design
Integration testing
practiceQuestions.explanation: The earlier a flaw is found, the cheaper it is to fix, and requirements and design come first. Integration testing is tempting because it finds real faults, but by then the parts have already been built.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two components each pass their own security tests. When they are joined, one trusts data from the other without checking it, which creates a weakness. In which stage should this be found?
options: Integration
Retirement
Requirements analysis
Stakeholder needs
practiceQuestions.explanation: Integration tests the connections between parts. Requirements analysis is tempting because it is an early check, but the weakness only exists once the parts have been joined.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A testing team checks each feature of a new system against the signed specification and confirms that all items pass. What activity have they completed?
options: Validation
Authorization
Certification of risk acceptance
Verification
practiceQuestions.explanation: Checking the system against written requirements is verification. Validation is tempting because it sounds similar, but validation checks the real needs of the users.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A new expense system meets every line of its specification, but staff report it does not match how the business really works. Which conclusion is BEST?
options: Verification has failed, and validation has passed
Verification has passed, and validation has failed
Both verification and validation have passed
Both verification and validation have failed
practiceQuestions.explanation: Meeting the specification means verification passed, and not meeting the real need means validation failed. The first option is tempting if the two terms are swapped, so remember that verification looks at the document.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Development has finished and testing has passed. Before going live, who should formally accept the remaining risk?
options: A senior manager with authority over the system
The lead developer who wrote the code
The tester who ran the final test
A representative of the vendor
practiceQuestions.explanation: Accepting risk is a decision for management. The lead developer is tempting because of technical knowledge, but technical staff do not have the authority to accept risk on behalf of the business.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An administrator makes an urgent, undocumented change to a production firewall to restore a service. What is the BEST next step under good change management?
options: Reverse the change right away, even if the service fails again
Leave the change alone, as the service has been restored
Submit the change for review and record it after the fact
Dismiss the administrator for failing to follow the process
practiceQuestions.explanation: Emergency changes can shorten the process, but they are still reviewed and recorded afterwards. Leaving it alone is tempting because the service works, but an unrecorded change is a hidden risk.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company is retiring a system. Which action should be done FIRST?
options: Wipe all of the server's disks
Remove the firewall rules for the system
Destroy the encryption keys
Check how long data must be retained
practiceQuestions.explanation: Retention requirements decide what must be kept, so this comes before anything is destroyed. Wiping the disks is tempting because it is the obvious task, but it could destroy records that the law requires.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company must sanitize solid state drives from a retired system. Which method should NOT be relied on?
options: Physical shredding of the drives
Degaussing the drives
Cryptographic erasure, if data was encrypted
A vendor-approved purge command
practiceQuestions.explanation: Degaussing relies on magnetic fields and does not work on solid state drives, which store data electronically. Cryptographic erasure is tempting to doubt, but destroying the keys is an accepted method if the data was properly encrypted.

examQuestions.prompt: A company moves its payroll to a SaaS (Software as a Service) product. Later, an attacker logs in to the company's account using a stolen password, because the company never turned on the multi-factor login that the product offers. Which party is responsible for this weakness?
options: The provider, because it hosts the application and the data
The provider, because it should detect any stolen password
The customer, because it controls its users and their access
Both are equally liable, because the contract covers the cloud
examQuestions.explanation: Under shared responsibility, the customer always manages its own users, access and settings. The provider answer is tempting because it runs the application, but the provider offered the protection and the customer chose not to use it.

examQuestions.prompt: A hospital wants to be sure that lab results can only be changed through one approved application, which checks each change, and that the person entering a result is not the one who approves it. Which model BEST fits this requirement?
options: Clark-Wilson
Bell-LaPadula
Brewer-Nash
Noninterference
examQuestions.explanation: Clark-Wilson forces all changes through approved programs and supports separation of duties. Bell-LaPadula is tempting because medical data is sensitive, but it protects confidentiality and does not address how data is changed.

examQuestions.prompt: A company wants its laptops' disk encryption keys tied to each laptop, and wants the disk to stay locked if someone tampers with the startup files. Which feature BEST meets this need?
options: A network-attached Hardware Security Module
A Trusted Platform Module in each laptop
Address Space Layout Randomization
A strong login password for each user
examQuestions.explanation: A TPM (Trusted Platform Module) stores keys on the device and releases them only if startup measurements match. An HSM (Hardware Security Module) is tempting because it guards keys, but it is built for central high-volume use and does not check each laptop's startup.

examQuestions.prompt: A new records system has passed all of its testing, and an independent assessor has delivered a technical report listing a few remaining low risks. The team wants to go live. What must happen NEXT?
options: The assessor signs a statement accepting the remaining risks
The developers fix every low risk before anyone can use it
The project manager schedules the go-live with the help desk
A senior manager formally accepts the remaining risk
examQuestions.explanation: Certification is technical, while authorization is a management decision to accept risk before transition to live use. The assessor option is tempting because the assessor knows the details, but only someone with authority over the business can accept its risk.

examQuestions.prompt: A water treatment plant finds a flaw in the software that runs its pump controllers. The vendor says the patch needs testing, and the plant cannot stop pumping this month. What is the BEST action for the security manager?
options: Tighten network separation and monitoring until patching is safe
Apply the patch tonight across every controller to close the flaw
Accept the risk and take no action until the next annual shutdown
Connect the controllers to the office network for central patching
examQuestions.explanation: In industrial systems, safety and availability come first, so reduce the risk with compensating controls while a patch is tested and planned. Patching at once is tempting, but an untested change could stop the pumps and endanger the public.

examQuestions.prompt: Two companies that have never exchanged a secret must transfer a very large file securely over the internet, as quickly as possible. Which approach is BEST?
options: Encrypt the whole file with the receiver's public RSA key
Encrypt the whole file with AES using ECB mode and a fixed key
Exchange a session key using public key methods, then use AES
Hash the whole file with SHA-256 and send the file with its hash
examQuestions.explanation: Hybrid encryption uses public key methods to share a symmetric key safely, then fast AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) for the bulk of the data. Using RSA alone is tempting because no shared secret is needed, but it is far too slow for large files.

examQuestions.prompt: A company encrypts its most important archive with one master key. The security manager wants the key to be recoverable if staff leave, but no single person should be able to recover it alone. Which control is BEST?
options: Give the key to the chief executive in a sealed envelope
Use M of N control, with parts held by several managers
Store a full copy of the key on each manager's laptop
Rotate the key every month and tell the system administrator
examQuestions.explanation: M of N control lets a set number of trusted people recover the key together, so no one person holds that power and one departure does not cause a loss. The sealed envelope is tempting, but it gives one person full control and creates a single point of failure.

examQuestions.prompt: An organization is hit by ransomware that has spread across several file servers. The incident response plan has been activated. What should the team do FIRST?
options: Isolate the affected systems to contain the spread
Pay the ransom quickly to reduce the time of the outage
Restore every server from backup as soon as possible
Wipe all staff computers and reinstall each operating system
examQuestions.explanation: Containment comes first, so isolate infected systems. Restoring from backup is tempting, but restoring before containment lets the malware encrypt the clean data again. Paying is a senior management decision and does not guarantee recovery.

examQuestions.prompt: A fire alarm sounds in a building. The server room door has an electronic lock, and the security team wants it to stay locked to protect the equipment. Staff are working inside at the time. What is the BEST approach for how this door should work?
options: It stays locked, to protect the equipment and the data inside
It stays locked until a guard arrives to escort the staff out
It stays locked unless a manager approves a remote release
It lets people inside leave freely during the emergency
examQuestions.explanation: People's safety always comes first, so a person inside must be able to get out, even when security is reduced. Waiting for a guard is tempting because it seems controlled, but any delay could cost lives.

examQuestions.prompt: A company runs its application as many small services in containers. An attacker took over one service and then freely reached all the others, because internal traffic was trusted automatically. Which design change is the BEST long-term fix?
options: Add a stronger firewall at the edge of the company's network
Authenticate every service call and allow only those required
Move every service back into one large single application
Scan all the container images once again before each release
examQuestions.explanation: Zero trust removes automatic trust inside the network, so each call is checked and only allowed where needed. A stronger edge firewall is tempting, but the attacker was already inside, and it does nothing to stop movement between services.

reviewSession.heading: Secure design: objective 3.1
reviewSession.body: Let us go back over Domain 3 together, one objective at a time, starting with secure design. Threat modeling happens early, and it is repeated when the system changes. Know the six STRIDE threats. Least privilege covers both the amount of access and the time it lasts. Defense in depth means different kinds of layers. Segregation of duties makes fraud need collusion. People often mix up fail-safe and fail-secure. Fail-safe unlocks to protect people. Fail-secure stays locked to protect assets. Zero trust checks every request, and never trusts by location, while the older trust but verify checks later. Shared responsibility splits the tasks, but you remain accountable for your own data. When choosing the best answer, prefer building security in at the start, and remember that whenever safety and security pull apart, people's safety wins.

reviewSession.heading: Security models: objective 3.2
reviewSession.body: Now the security models. This is where exact wording matters most. Bell-LaPadula protects secrets. Its simple property is no read up, and its star property is no write down. Biba protects correctness, and its rules are the reverse. Its simple property is no read down, and its star property is no write up. Simple is always about reading, and star is always about writing. Clark-Wilson forces every change through an approved program, using the access triple of subject, program and object, along with separation of duties. Brewer-Nash reacts to what you have already seen, in order to prevent conflicts of interest. Take-Grant shows how rights can be passed along. Noninterference says that high level actions must not be visible at low levels. People mix up the two main models under pressure, so when a question arrives, ask first what is being protected. Is it secrets, correctness, or a conflict of interest? The answer points to the model.

reviewSession.heading: Requirements and evaluation: objective 3.3
reviewSession.body: Next comes choosing controls and evaluating products. Always start from requirements, never from a favourite product. Functional requirements say what a control must do. Assurance requirements say how sure we are that it works. Common Criteria uses three terms. The Protection Profile is what a type of customer needs. The Security Target is what the vendor claims. The Target of Evaluation is the exact thing tested. Learn the seven Evaluation Assurance Levels in order, from functionally tested at level one, to formally verified design and tested at level seven. The trap that catches people most is thinking that a higher level means more features. It means deeper testing against stated claims, for one exact configuration. Certification is technical. Authorization is management accepting the risk. So if a question asks who decides whether a system may go live, the answer is a senior manager, and not the assessor who tested it.

reviewSession.heading: System capabilities: objective 3.4
reviewSession.body: Now the security capabilities of systems. The Trusted Computing Base is everything that enforces security, and it should be small. A reference monitor is the concept of checking every access. It must be tamperproof, always invoked and verifiable. The security kernel is the real implementation of that concept. If a question says concept, choose reference monitor. If it says actual components, choose security kernel. Process isolation keeps programs apart, and a lower protection ring number means more power, so Ring 0 is the kernel. Address Space Layout Randomization hides where things are in memory, and Data Execution Prevention stops code running from data areas. People often confuse the two key-protecting devices. A Trusted Platform Module is a chip that protects one machine and checks its startup. A Hardware Security Module serves many keys at high volume. Finally, secure enclaves protect data in use, which is the hardest state to protect.

reviewSession.heading: Vulnerabilities in architectures: objective 3.5
reviewSession.body: Now weaknesses by type of system. Aggregation combines low-value facts into something sensitive. Inference works out a secret from what you may see. Polyinstantiation keeps different versions of a record for different clearances. In industrial systems, safety and availability come first, so an untested patch is rarely the best answer. Separate those systems, and treat smart devices as untrusted. Covert channels have a deliberate sender, while side channels have only an observer. In the cloud, the customer patches the operating system under Infrastructure as a Service, while the provider does so under Platform and Software as a Service. The customer always owns its data and access, and accountability can never be handed over. Containers share one kernel, so they are less isolated than virtual machines. A Type 1 hypervisor runs on the hardware. When two answers both help, choose the one that fits this particular system.

reviewSession.heading: Symmetric cryptography: objective 3.6
reviewSession.body: Let us go over symmetric encryption, where the numbers are tested directly. One shared key does both jobs, it is fast, and it cannot give non-repudiation. To count the keys, take the number of people, multiply by one less than that number, and divide by two. Ten people need ten times nine, which is ninety, divided by two, which is forty-five keys. Asymmetric needs two keys per person, so ten people need twenty. Data Encryption Standard, or DES, has a 64-bit block, a 56-bit key and 16 rounds. Triple DES has 48 rounds, and three keys give about 112 bits of real strength. The Advanced Encryption Standard always has a 128-bit block. Its 128, 192 and 256-bit keys use 10, 12 and 14 rounds. Avoid Electronic Codebook mode, because patterns show. Galois Counter Mode gives secrecy and integrity together. The most common slip is forgetting to divide by two.

reviewSession.heading: Asymmetric cryptography and signatures: objective 3.6
reviewSession.body: Now asymmetric keys, hashes and signatures. Ask what the goal is. For secrecy, encrypt with the receiver's public key, and the receiver decrypts with the private key. To sign, the sender uses the sender's own private key, and anyone verifies with the sender's public key. A digital signature hashes the message, and protects that hash with the private key. It gives integrity, authentication and non-repudiation, but it does not give confidentiality. HMAC uses a shared key, so it gives integrity and authenticity, but not non-repudiation. Hashing is one-way and gives integrity only. Diffie-Hellman agrees a key, but it does not prove identity by itself. Real systems are hybrid, so a public key method sets up a fast symmetric session key. In quantum matters, Shor's algorithm threatens public key methods, while Grover's roughly halves symmetric strength. If an answer has someone sharing a private key, it is almost certainly wrong.

reviewSession.heading: PKI and key management: objective 3.6
reviewSession.body: Now Public Key Infrastructure and key management. The Certificate Authority issues and signs. The Registration Authority only checks identity. The root is kept offline, and intermediates do the daily work. A certificate binds a public key to a name, and a private key is never inside one. Be very clear about revocation. A Certificate Revocation List is a signed list that is published from time to time, and it can be large and out of date. The Online Certificate Status Protocol is a live question about one certificate. Stapling lets the server attach a recent signed answer. If a private key is stolen, revoke first, and then issue a new certificate with a new key pair. Keys have a lifecycle from generation to destruction, and rotation limits the damage. Split knowledge, dual control and M of N all stop one person from holding full power.

reviewSession.heading: Cryptanalytic attacks: objective 3.7
reviewSession.body: Now the attacks. Mathematical attacks are named after what the attacker holds: ciphertext only, known plaintext, chosen plaintext and chosen ciphertext. Frequency analysis breaks simple substitution. The birthday attack finds hash collisions. Do not confuse meet in the middle, which is the reason Double DES failed, with man in the middle, which is an attack on a live conversation. Side-channel attacks and timing attacks only observe. Fault injection actively disturbs. In pass the hash, the attacker uses a stolen hash and never needs the password, so longer passwords do not solve it. In Kerberos, the golden ticket needs the KRBTGT hash and controls the domain, the silver ticket needs a service account hash and reaches one service, and Kerberoasting cracks a service account's password offline. For ransomware, tested offline backups are the best preparation. Isolate infected systems first, and leave the decision to pay with senior management.

reviewSession.heading: Site and facility design: objective 3.8
reviewSession.body: Next, site and facility design. Physical security starts before anything is built, so assess the site first. Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design has three strategies. Natural access control guides people. Natural surveillance lets people see and be seen. Natural territorial reinforcement shows that the place is owned and cared for. Zones become stricter the deeper you go. Think in the order of deter, deny, detect, delay and respond, and remember that barriers need to hold an intruder for as long as the response takes to arrive. A mantrap stops tailgating. Put server rooms near the centre of a building, on a middle floor, away from water and outside walls, and run the walls to the true ceiling. In the exam, when a question offers a low-cost change to the design of a place alongside a costly guard or a new device, the design change is usually the better answer.

reviewSession.heading: Site and facility controls: objective 3.9
reviewSession.body: Now site and facility controls, which carry several exact lists. For power, short problems are fault, sag and spike, and long ones are blackout, brownout and surge. Fire classes are A for ordinary items, B for liquids, C for live electrical equipment, D for metals and K for kitchen oils. Never use water on live electrical equipment. For sprinklers, wet pipe is always full, dry pipe suits freezing places, deluge opens every head at once, and preaction needs a detector and then a melted head, which makes it the best water choice for data centres. Carbon dioxide can kill, so it needs an empty room or a warning delay. Too little humidity causes static, and too much causes corrosion. Evidence needs an unbroken chain of custody. And the rule that overrides all of these is that protecting people always comes before protecting equipment.

reviewSession.heading: The system lifecycle: objective 3.10
reviewSession.body: Finally, the information system lifecycle. Learn the nine stages in order: stakeholder needs, requirements analysis, architectural design, development, integration, verification and validation, transition, operations and maintenance, and retirement. Security belongs in every one of them, and the earliest fix is the cheapest. The distinction that is tested most often is this one. Verification asks whether we built it right, and checks the system against the written requirements. Validation asks whether we built the right thing, and checks it against the real needs of the users. A system can pass the first and fail the second. A senior manager approves going live. Operations is usually the longest stage, and every change is reviewed, approved, tested and recorded. At retirement, check how long data must be kept before you destroy anything. Across the whole domain, think like a manager, fix the cause, follow policy, and put people's safety first.
